0.title: The Case-Book
0.description: Five volumes lie on the corner of the table at 221B, in the lamp-light, in Watson's bad handwriting and your own good paper. The thick black one is the case that you will remember: it is the whole of a winter and a spring, and it is not finished with you. The four thinner ones are the smaller cases, each done in a day or a week, each complete in itself. Any of them can be opened. None of them depends on any other, and what you do in one will not follow you into the next.

options.label: The Final Problem. London, 1891.
options.detail: The major case: the Professor, the Yard, the boys in the street, your brother's club and the road to the Falls. A long story with four roads, six meters and a good many endings. Play it first, if you like, or last.
options.outcome: You take down the black volume and open it at the first page. It smells of pipe-smoke and fog.

options.label: The Speckled Band. Stoke Moran, 1883.
options.detail: A minor case: a frightened girl, a locked bedroom and a dead sister's last word. Four scenes, four endings, one of them hidden.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I do not think I have ever been so frightened in my life as I was that night. I am glad that I wrote it down, if only to prove that I was.

options.outcome: You take down the thin green volume. A slip of paper marks a page that Watson has not been able to read since.

options.label: A Scandal in Bohemia. London, 1888.
options.detail: A minor case: a King in a mask, a photograph in a strongbox, and the one woman who ever beat you. Four scenes, four endings, one of them hidden.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: A mask, a King and a lady. It is the sort of thing that I should be ashamed to have written, if it were not so true.

options.outcome: You take down the thin yellow volume. It is the one with the pressed violet in it.

options.label: The Blue Carbuncle. Christmas, 1889.
options.detail: A minor case, and cheerful: a battered hat, a Christmas goose and a stone worth more than twenty thousand pounds. Four scenes, four endings, one of them hidden.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I am told that it is the only one of your cases that ends with anybody being forgiven. I thought you might like to be reminded.

options.outcome: You take down the thin red volume. There is a goose feather between the pages.

options.label: The Red-Headed League. Saxe-Coburg Square, 1890.
options.detail: A minor case, the lightest of the five: a pawnbroker, four pounds a week and a good reason to copy out the Encyclopaedia. Four scenes, four endings, one of them hidden.
options.outcome: You take down the thin orange volume. There is a single red hair between the pages, wiry.

1.title: The First Thread
1.description: Sunday 4 January 1891. The first snow of the year has been trodden grey outside 221B Baker Street, and the Sunday papers lie where you flung them. Three small misfortunes, in three divisions of the police, have wandered into your notebook this week. A forged bill of exchange has passed through a discount house in Cornhill without a blemish. A clerk in Lombard Street has been taken out of the river, and the inquest has called it despair. A strongroom in Hatton Garden has been opened and emptied, and no tool has touched the lock. No one else sees a line between them. You see one cool hand behind all three, and you do not yet know whose it is.

options.label: Follow the Forged Bill Through the Discount Houses.
options.detail: Weeks of dull, patient work in the City, one signature at a time.

quote.speaker: Mr Pollard, discount broker
quote.text: A good hand, sir. Too good. Whoever drew it has never once made the mistake a forger makes.

options.outcome: The bill leads you through six houses and four counting-rooms, and every trail ends at a different respectable name with no past. That, you decide, is the signature: clean names, built the way other men build fences.

options.label: Lay All Three Cases Before Lestrade at the Yard.
options.detail: Open a joint file. It costs you the pleasure of working unobserved.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Three cases, three divisions, three different men on them. I can't say I see the link, Mr Holmes. But I'll not say you're wrong.

options.outcome: Lestrade copies out the particulars in his square hand and promises to read them twice. It is more than the Yard has ever given one of your theories at the first sitting. A file is opened, and with it a door you may need later.

options.label: Draw the Curtains and Work From the Papers Alone.
options.detail: Cuttings, ledgers, inquest reports. No one to interrupt, and no one to share it with.

quote.speaker: Mrs Hudson
quote.text: He's not had a proper meal since Thursday, sir, and now he's asking me for the tobacco from the Persian slipper.

options.outcome: For three days the room is blue with smoke and the floor is white with paper. When you open the curtains at last the pattern is plain on the wall: a hundred small crimes, and one patient mind that has never been seen in any of them.

2.title: A Name in the Margin
2.description:
Friday 23 January. The pattern has a centre now, and the centre has a name. It was pencilled in the margin of the drowned clerk's pocket-book, and nowhere else in London is it written down: James Moriarty. A former professor of mathematics. Author, at twenty-one, of a treatise on the binomial theorem that earned him a European reputation and a chair at a provincial university.

He left it under circumstances no one will explain, and he now lives in London on a modest income, coaching officers for the Army. He has no record, no debts and no enemies. You find that last fact the most alarming of all.

options.label: Ask Mycroft What the Government Knows of the Man.
options.detail: A call at the Diogenes Club. Your brother gives nothing for nothing.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: I know of him as one knows of the weather, Sherlock. One does not ask who is responsible for it. One only notes that it has been mild for a long time.

options.outcome: Mycroft listens with his eyes shut, then names three departments that have quietly stopped asking questions about the Professor. He does not say why. He says only that if you require him, you will find that he can be required.

options.label: Call on the Professor Under the Pretext of a Lecture Enquiry.
options.detail: Meet him face to face. He will study you as closely as you study him.

quote.speaker: A maid in Moriarty's hall
quote.text: The Professor will see you in the study, sir. He asks if you will be so kind as to take the chair by the lamp.

success.outcome: He is courteous, hollow-cheeked, and still but for a slow swaying of the head. You leave with nothing he meant to give, but you carry out the shape of the room, the cabinet he did not look at, and the name of the tutor who comes on Thursdays.

failure.outcome: He is courteous. He is also three steps ahead of every question, and by the time you take your leave you understand that the visit has told him more about you than it told you about him. There is a lamp lit in an upper window as you cross the street.

options.label: Say Nothing and Watch His House From a Hired Room.
options.detail: A fortnight of cold tea and field-glasses. Slow, and a little expensive.

quote.speaker: The landlady opposite
quote.text: You'll be wanting the room by the week, then, sir? You'll not be bringing company? The last gentleman who watched that house was gone by Easter.

options.outcome: You learn the names of his visitors by their hats, and the hours of his house by its lamps. Nobody at all comes who is not tall, quiet and well-dressed, and nobody leaves with a parcel. You are beginning to think it is the best-kept house in London.

options.label: Pawn the Violin for a Fortnight's Expenses.
options.detail: A good instrument, and a bad bargain. You will have it back by Easter, if the Professor allows.

quote.speaker: The pawnbroker
quote.text: A Stradivari, sir? I'll give you ten pounds on the strength of the case alone. I never could tell a good fiddle from a bad one. I can tell a gentleman in want.

options.outcome: The pawnbroker looks at the violin for a long minute with an expression you cannot read, and writes out the ticket in a small hand. You walk out into the street with ten pounds in your pocket and an unfamiliar lightness at your shoulder. Mrs Hudson, that evening, does not mention the empty place on the shelf.

3.title: The Brick on Vere Street
3.description: Monday 9 February. You are walking down Vere Street, thinking of nothing but the Professor's cabinet, when a brick comes down from the roof of one of the houses and breaks to fragments at your feet. A hand's breadth to the left and your case would have been a matter for the coroner. It was not thrown; it was dropped, from a man who knew the hour you pass and the side of the street you keep. You look up. The skyline is empty, and the whole street seems to be listening.

options.label: Go Up After Him Over the Rooftops.
options.detail: He has half a minute's start. You have a good head for heights and a poor one for caution.

quote.speaker: A constable in Vere Street
quote.text: Mind the slates, sir! That chimney's been loose since Michaelmas!

success.outcome: He is a thick-set man in a cabman's coat, and he goes down a drainpipe like a sailor. You do not catch him, but you catch his name from the porter who shouted after him: Fitch, who drives for hire at a yard in Kentish Town. At last, a real thread to hold.

failure.outcome: A slate gives under your boot, and you hang by one hand over the street while a crowd collects below. You are fetched down by a ladder, and the constable takes your name with some satisfaction. The man on the roof is somewhere in Marylebone, laughing.

options.label: Report It at the Station and Have the Roof Searched.
options.detail: Do the dull and proper thing, and put it on the record.

quote.speaker: The station sergeant
quote.text: A brick, Mr Holmes? Dropped on purpose? We'll send two men up. Though I'll tell you plainly, we get a deal of bricks.

options.outcome: Two constables search the roof and find a clay pipe, a footprint and an ordinary view. But the report is written down, and it bears your name and the date. If anything should happen to you, a clerk at the Yard will know it was not an accident.

options.label: Walk On and Say Nothing.
options.detail: Let the man on the roof think you did not even look up.

quote.speaker: A passing flower girl
quote.text: Lord, sir, did you see that? Right on top of you! You never so much as jumped!

options.outcome: You step around the fragments and go on to your appointment at the same pace as before. It is a cold little performance, and it is meant for an audience. Whoever dropped the brick will report that you are not frightened. You hope he is a poor judge.

options.label: Leave the Rooftop and Read the Note That Came This Morning.
options.detail: It was on violet paper, scented, and signed with two initials. It has been in your pocket-book since breakfast, unopened, like a small unexploded shell.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Holmes, you have been staring at that envelope for a quarter of an hour. It is not a cipher. It is a lady's handwriting, and I rather think you know whose.

options.outcome: You read it standing at the corner of Vere Street with the brick still in your other hand.

echoes.text: The man on the roof did not choose you by chance. Since your visit to the Professor's house you have been a name on someone's list.

4.title: The Napoleon of Crime
4.description: Tuesday 17 February. In Lestrade's room at Scotland Yard the fire smokes and the clock ticks, and your theory sounds, even to yourself, a little like a ghost story. You have no single crime to put on the table. You have a hundred, and they share a style that only you can read. There is a man, you say, who has never been charged with anything, who sits at the centre of the web like a spider, and who is to crime what Napoleon was to war. Lestrade does not laugh. But he looks at the door as though he were afraid his Chief might come in.

options.label: Lay Out the Whole Pattern: Forgeries, Deaths, and a Man Never Charged.
options.detail: Everything you have, in the order you found it. A bold stroke, and it either lands or it does not.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: If you're right, Mr Holmes, then every one of us has been looking at the same man for ten years and calling him a coincidence.

success.outcome: Lestrade reads for an hour, and when he looks up his face has changed. He asks for a copy, and then for a second copy to keep in his own drawer. By Friday the file has a number, and a red ribbon, and the Chief Inspector's initials.

failure.outcome: You had meant to astonish him with the sweep of it. Instead you overwhelm him, and he hears only the extravagance. 'It's ingenious,' he says, which in the Yard means that it is impossible. Word goes down the corridor, and you leave the building to a murmur of laughter.

options.label: Offer Lestrade One Small, Certain Arrest as Proof of Good Faith.
options.detail: Hand him a lieutenant on a plate. It spends a thread, but it buys a friend.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: I'll take him, Mr Holmes, and I'll be grateful. Though I notice you give me the little fish and keep the pond to yourself.

options.outcome: A receiver in Whitechapel is taken that night with the forged bills still in his coat. The Yard has its arrest, and you have given up a link in your chain to get it. Lestrade shakes your hand with real warmth. The pond, he reminds you, will wait.

options.label: Leave the Yard Out of It.
options.detail: A building full of clerks is a building that talks. You will go on alone.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Have it your own way, Mr Holmes. But when you come to us for a warrant, don't expect us to remember who it was that kept us out.

options.outcome: You say only that the matter is not ripe. Lestrade nods slowly and writes nothing down. It is a courteous dismissal, and you both know it. You have kept your secret, and lost a little of a friendship you did not know you were spending.

options.label: Offer to Take a Case the Yard Cannot Spare a Man For.
options.detail: A small matter that has been sitting on Lestrade's desk for a month. It earns goodwill, and costs a week.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: There's a coachman in the cells at Marylebone, Mr Holmes, and a book gone missing from Clerkenwell, and a young lady who keeps writing to us about letters. I've nobody to give them to. If you'd care to look at one, I'd not say no.

options.outcome: Lestrade pushes a small pile of papers across the desk with an expression of unconcealed relief. It is a modest favour. A policeman remembers that sort.

echoes.text: Lestrade already has the first file open on his desk. Today he wants to know why it has grown so thick.

5.title: Wiggins and the Boys
5.description: Monday 2 March. A knock on the sitting-room door, and then a smell of coal-smoke and boot-blacking: Wiggins, the leader of the street boys you call the Baker Street Irregulars, with his cap in both hands. He has heard that you are working on something large. The boys, he says, can go where the police cannot, and be unseen where a gentleman cannot, because nobody in London sees a ragged child. They want a shilling a day each, and they want to know whom they are following.

options.label: Hire the Whole Gang by the Week.
options.detail: A dozen pairs of eyes on every corner. It will cost you money, and it will cost you the right to say you didn't know.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: We'll have him, Mr Holmes, whoever he is. Only don't tell us he's a gentleman, because the gentlemen's the ones that never see us.

options.outcome: Twelve boys vanish into the foggy street like a handful of coins thrown into a pond. By Saturday you know the hours of a dozen houses, the names of three cab-yards, and the colour of a particular dog-cart that has been seen too often near Lombard Street.

options.label: Take Wiggins Himself, for One Errand Only.
options.detail: The smallest net you can cast. Cheap, careful, and not wide.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: One job and one boy, sir? Well. It's a poor sort of a gang that can only do one job. But you're paying, and I'm the best boy there is.

options.outcome: Wiggins returns in two days with the address of a printer in Clerkenwell and a look of wounded pride. You thank him, pay him, and send him home. It is safe, and it is quiet, and it does not feel like a war.

options.label: Send Them Away and Trust Your Own Eyes.
options.detail: Children should not carry the weight of this. You will carry it yourself.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: Suit yourself, Mr Holmes. But you'll be wanting us sooner than you think.

options.outcome: You give him sixpence for his trouble and a lecture you suspect he does not want. It is kindly meant, and you know even as the door closes that you have made your own work heavier. For a fortnight you are everywhere yourself, in a different coat each night.

6.title: The Frightened Clerk
6.description: Sunday 15 March, near midnight. A man has been standing under the lamp across the road for an hour, and when you open the door he comes over the street almost at a run. He is young, and ill-dressed for the cold, and he has the white face of one who has not slept since Christmas. His name is Tobias Larch. He is a clerk in the bank that clears the Professor's bills, and he has understood what he has been signing. He wants to talk. He also wants, with great earnestness, not to be dead by Friday.

options.label: Take Larch Into Baker Street and Keep Him There.
options.detail: Give him your own sitting-room and your own protection. If the Professor's men find him, you will have invited them.

quote.speaker: Tobias Larch
quote.text: I would sooner be in your room with the door barred than in the street with a pocket full of money. I can tell you where they keep the ledger.

success.outcome: You sit up with him until the grey comes into the windows. Mrs Hudson brings him broth and no questions. By morning you have three hours of statement in your notebook, and a young man who has begun to believe he may live.

failure.outcome: He is in your armchair, halfway through his second cup, when a stone breaks the window and a voice in the street shouts something that makes him stand up and put on his hat. You cannot hold him. You reach the stairs a moment after the door has closed, and you catch only the hurrying shape of him in the fog.

options.label: Hear Him Out on the Pavement, Then Send Him Home.
options.detail: Get the statement quickly and let him go back to his lodgings. A man who vanishes is noticed. A man who goes to work is not.

quote.speaker: Tobias Larch
quote.text: You'll send me back, then? To Lombard Street? Well. I suppose you know best, Mr Holmes. You know best about everything.

options.outcome: He talks for twenty minutes under the lamp, in a whisper, and you commit it to memory. Then you put him in a cab. You do not ask yourself, until the morning, what you ought to have asked yourself at once: why a man watched for a month should be allowed to go home alone.

options.label: Send Him to Lestrade With a Note.
options.detail: Put the man in the Yard's keeping and the matter on the record.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Send him round, Mr Holmes. I'll put a man on the door myself, and one at the back. Nobody gets at a witness of mine.

options.outcome: Lestrade's man collects Larch within the hour, and the witness is housed in a police lodging with two constables on the stair. The statement is taken down by a shorthand clerk. It is formal, correct, and admissible in any court in England.

echoes.text: Lestrade has already said at the Yard that you will be 'looking into' a bank clerk. It was not a thing he ought to have said.
Wiggins's boys have been on the corner for a week, and one of them saw Larch under the lamp before you did.
A cipher from Whitehall is in your inside pocket. It says, in nine words, that someone at the Bank has been careless.
Your papers lie all over the carpet and nobody has seen you in daylight for a week. Larch, who has been watching the house, has been afraid to knock.

7.title: What Larch Knew
7.description: Wednesday 18 March. Larch has talked for a day and a night, and what he has told you is larger than you dared hope. The Professor does not give orders. He sends no letters and keeps no accounts that any court could read. But there is one book, the clerk says, a ledger bound in grey cloth, in which the Professor reckons the whole business in a private cipher: every debt, every favour, every name. It is kept in a locked cabinet in the coaching establishment off the Marylebone Road. If you can put that book on a magistrate's table, there is no jury in London that could acquit him.

options.label: Break Into the Coaching House and Take the Ledger.
options.detail: One night, one lock, and no one the wiser. If it goes wrong, you will have broken the law to catch someone who never did.

quote.speaker: Tobias Larch
quote.text: The cabinet is behind the clock in the back room. He winds that clock himself, every evening at nine. Don't be there at nine.

success.outcome: The lock is a good one and you have a better pick. The ledger is where Larch said, wrapped in a baize cloth, and you are across the road and away before the clock behind you has done striking one. In a cab on the Marylebone Road you open it by the light of a match. It is all there, in a hand so neat that it has the look of a work of art.

failure.outcome: The door is bolted on a second lock you were not told about. You are halfway through it when a light goes up in the house and a tutor in a dressing-gown comes down with a poker. You come out through a coal-hole, with a torn coat and no ledger, and by morning the break-in is in the Marylebone divisional book.

options.label: Have Lestrade Obtain a Warrant to Search the House.
options.detail: Slow, formal and lawful. The ledger will be in the Yard's hands, not yours, and the Professor will see them coming.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: If we do it by the book, Mr Holmes, then we'll have it by the book. Nobody can stand up in court and say we cheated.

success.outcome: A magistrate with a dislike of coaching establishments signs the warrant on the second reading. The ledger is lifted by the Yard in daylight, listed, signed for, and stored behind two locks at Scotland Yard. It will bear the weight of any cross-examination.

failure.outcome: The warrant arrives on the Friday, and on the Friday the house is a boarding-house for six respectable tutors and a cat. The cabinet is gone from behind the clock. Somewhere in the Yard, a door was opened that should have been kept shut.

options.label: Copy Only What Larch Can Recite, and Hold the Rest.
options.detail: Leave the ledger where it is. Build the case from the clerk's own memory, and trust your own.

quote.speaker: Tobias Larch
quote.text: I can give you the first forty pages by heart, Mr Holmes. After that it becomes a matter of figures I only saw once.

options.outcome: You write until the lamp is low, and Larch dictates until his voice is gone. It is a thin, secondhand account, and the Professor's counsel will tear at it in court. But it is safe, and it is lawful, and nobody has been hurt in the getting of it.

echoes.text: Larch sits in your armchair with a rug about his knees. He has been talking since the lamps were lit, and between sentences he looks at the door.
Lestrade has offered, already, to see you through a magistrate. It is a thing that you would not have had in January.
Wiggins knows the coaching house. The boys have counted its windows, and its drains, and the cat.
Whitehall has a file on that coaching house, and has not shown you the file.
You know the house by its roof and its drains, and have drawn it twice on the back of your own cipher.

8.title: Watson's Surgery
8.description:
Saturday 28 March. You have not been to Kensington in a month. Watson is in his consulting-room, in shirt-sleeves, with a ledger of his own, and he looks up and says nothing for a moment. He has been a doctor for three years since his marriage and a friend for much longer, and he reads your face as another man might read a newspaper.

There are lines in it that were not there at Christmas. He puts down his pen and asks, with the careful kindness of his profession, whether you have been taking enough sleep, and whether you have been taking anything else.

options.label: Tell Him Everything.
options.detail: The Professor, the ledger, the brick, the dead clerk. He will be in danger the moment he knows.
options.outcome: It takes two hours, and he interrupts only to ask for water. When it is over he is silent, and then he takes his bag from the cupboard and begins to check it, with an air of settling the matter. 'I shall want my revolver cleaned,' he says. 'And you shall eat something.'

options.label: Tell Him Enough to Be Careful.
options.detail: The danger, but not the details. He will know to lock his doors.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are telling me to be careful and not to ask why. I do not like it. But I have known you too long to refuse.

options.outcome: He promises to keep his wife away from the street at night, and to send you a line if any strange man should call. He does not press you. He looks, at the end, a little hurt, and a little relieved, and you cannot say which you would have preferred.

options.label: Say Nothing. He Has a Wife and a Practice.
options.detail: He is the best man you know, and the first the Professor would reach for. Keep him away from it.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Oh, nothing's the matter, I dare say. You always look like that when you have a case. But do come to dinner, Holmes. Mary would be glad.

options.outcome: You eat a little, say less, and take your leave at nine. In the hall he catches your sleeve. 'If it should ever be anything,' he says, and stops. You tell him it is not. You have not lied to him so plainly in ten years, and you keep hearing it all the way back to Baker Street.

echoes.text: He glances at the black bag by your hand, and then at your fingers. 'You have not been using the morocco case again,' he says, in the voice he keeps for patients.
The Yard's fires are warm, and its doors are open. You find that you are not afraid of them.
Your boots are wet from three nights on the quay, and there is a smell of tar on your coat that Watson does not remark upon.
You have a Foreign Office card in your breast pocket, and the odd, unfamiliar sensation of having been taken seriously.
You have not been out of the house in five days, and you are aware that Watson has noticed.

9.title: A Dray at the Corner
9.description: Saturday 11 April. You step off the pavement in Welbeck Street and a two-horse van comes round the corner at a gallop, driverless in appearance, with a whip cracking from somewhere in the shadow of the box. You throw yourself back, and the wheel passes within a hair of your coat. A moment later the van has turned into Wigmore Street and is gone. This is the second attempt, and the first was clumsy. This was close. He is no longer trying to frighten you, you understand. He has begun to be impatient.

options.label: Let the Papers Report You Dead for a Week.
options.detail: A short obituary, a quiet notice, and a pair of eyes that might relax. If the trick is seen through, you will look a fool.

quote.speaker: The Standard's night editor
quote.text: I can put it in the Monday edition, Mr Holmes, if you give me a sentence. But if you turn out to be alive on Tuesday, I shall have a great many letters.

success.outcome: For six days nobody follows you. The Professor's men fall back into their old habits, and you are able to note which cab-ranks they use, which public-houses, and which letters they carry to which doors. When you walk into Scotland Yard on the seventh day, there is a satisfactory pause.

failure.outcome: The notice is read by everyone but the man for whom it was written. Your friends mourn, your landlady weeps and your brother sends a coolly worded note. The only effect on the enemy is that two of his men stop troubling to hide.

options.label: Post Wiggins's Boys on Every Corner of Baker Street.
options.detail: A dozen eyes on the street, day and night. The enemy will learn how thin the margin is.
options.outcome: The boys settle on the doorsteps and the area railings like sparrows. You are never alone in the street again, and you are never watched without being watched back. Mrs Hudson, at least, is satisfied that the milk is safe.

options.label: Move Into Watson's Spare Room for the Week.
options.detail: A different street, a quiet house, and a friend who sleeps with a revolver under his pillow.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You may have the back bedroom, and Mary will see that you are fed. I shall not ask whom you are hiding from. I shall simply sit up.

options.outcome: For the first time in three months you sleep for nine hours, and you wake to the smell of bacon and the sound of a carpet-beater in the next garden. The peace is extraordinary, and you are aware that it is borrowed.

options.label: Take a Cab Everywhere and Trust No Street.
options.detail: A dull answer to a sharp threat. Safe enough, and you will not have to explain it to anyone.

quote.speaker: Cabman at the rank
quote.text: Different cab every time, you say, sir? Well, it's your money. I'd have thought a gentleman would sooner walk.

options.outcome: You hire eleven cabs in six days. By the end you know the men of three ranks by name, and one of them, a drowsy old fellow with a sherry nose, has told you something about a certain yard in Kentish Town that you did not know. It is an expensive way to be careful.

options.label: Sell a Case-Book to a Collector.
options.detail: Three years of notes, in your own hand, bought by a collector who has promised never to read them. It is a short-sighted bargain, and a necessary one.

quote.speaker: A collector
quote.text: I shall keep it under glass, Mr Holmes, and never let it out of the house. I am told that a good detective's notes are better than a good novel. I shall be glad to put it to the test.

options.outcome: The collector counts out eight pounds in gold, and carries away the third volume of your case-books as though he had been given the Crown Jewels. You do not look back at the shelf. It is a short, sharp, shameful transaction, and you will make a great effort to forget it.

echoes.text: In the street you keep seeing a young man's white face under a lamp, and hearing him ask whether you know best about everything.

10.title: The Professor Calls
10.description: Friday 24 April, a little after eleven in the morning. Mrs Hudson has gone out for the fish, and you are alone in the sitting-room when the door opens without a knock and a tall, thin man walks in as though he had been there all his life. His forehead domes out in a white curve, and his deep-set eyes are watchful, and his head oscillates slowly from side to side like a reptile's. He sits down without being asked. You have never seen him before in your life, and you have known him for three months. 'You have less frontal development than I should have expected,' says Professor Moriarty.

options.label: Give Him Nothing. Let Him Say His Piece and Show Him the Door.
options.detail: A man like this has come to learn something, not to give it. Deny him the lesson.

quote.speaker: Professor Moriarty
quote.text: All that I have to say has already crossed your mind. You will find that the answer to it has crossed mine.

options.outcome: You listen to the whole of his speech with your fingertips together, and when it is over you rise and ring for the door. He leaves as he came, unhurried, and you stand at the window a long while after the street has swallowed him. You have refused him everything, and you are shaking a little. You think he knows.

options.label: Probe Him With a Question Only the Guilty Man Would Answer Wrongly.
options.detail: A single sentence, dropped in like a stone. If it lands, it may tell you more than a month of watching.

quote.speaker: Professor Moriarty
quote.text: You are ingenious, Mr Holmes. I am sorry to be the one to tell you that I am not a man who can be caught by ingenuity.

success.outcome: He answers too smoothly, and in the smoothness there is a gap: a name he should not have known, a date he should not have remembered. You say nothing at all, and your face does not move. When he has gone you write it down, word for word, before you forget the sound of it.

failure.outcome: He answers the question before you finish it, and in answering it he lets you see that he had expected it. His smile is brief and bloodless. When he has gone you find that you have given him a great deal and taken nothing, and your hands are colder than the day.

options.label: Take His Measure and Let Him See That You Fear Nothing.
options.detail: Answer calm with calm, and cold with colder. If he wants a duel, he shall have a gentleman's.

quote.speaker: Professor Moriarty
quote.text: You stand in my way, Mr Holmes. I am a patient man, but there is a limit to what even I can endure. I do not propose to repeat this visit.

options.outcome: He says it quietly, and you reply in kind, and neither of you raises his voice. In all the history of Baker Street, no war has been declared so courteously. When the door closes, you find your hand on the back of the chair, and a certainty in your mind that one of you will not see the summer.

options.label: Hear What He Would Give If You Were to Drop the Matter.
options.detail: It costs nothing to listen. It might cost a great deal to remember what you heard.

quote.speaker: Professor Moriarty
quote.text: There is a figure which would permit you to live in any city you chose, and never to hear my name again. I am curious to learn yours.

options.outcome: He names it. It is large. You say nothing, and he nods as though you had agreed to something, and goes. You do not tell anyone, then or afterwards, that for the space of one long breath you were interested.

echoes.text: He did not trouble to ask where you lived. He has known since January, and he tells you so as one pays a tradesman his due.
His glance goes to your coat pocket, once, and then away. He knows what you took from the back room, and he will not mention it. That is the most frightening part.
The Yard's men are already moving, and the Professor knows it. It is the only reason that he has come.
The boys are outside, in the area, twelve small faces at twelve small windows. He has, you think, counted them.
Whitehall's men are watching the street. The Professor has seen them, and he has come anyway, which tells you something.
He is not at all surprised to find you alone. He remarks on it, with the interest of a collector.

As he goes, on the landing, a tall man in a long coat steps aside to let him pass, with an odd-shaped stick under his arm, and lifts his hat to you. You have never seen him before. You will be a long time forgetting him.

11.title: Bruised Knuckles
11.description:
Friday 24 April, evening. Watson is smoking over the fire when you come in, as you have come in three times in a year, through the garden and over the wall, with a face the colour of paper. Your knuckles are bleeding. You tell him that you have been attacked twice more today, and that on Monday the police will close their hands upon the whole of the Professor's gang, if you can keep your own life until then.

You chose your road in February. Tonight is the night to be sure of it, or to change it, and to learn whether the door you chose has been kept open for you.

options.label: Stay in London and Hold to the Law. Scotland Yard, on Monday, With You at the Table.
options.detail: The road of proof. It stays open if you chose it in February, or if the Yard still trusts you now.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Come to the Yard in the morning, Mr Holmes. Bring everything. If we're going to do it, we'll do it on one night, and we'll do it properly.

options.outcome: You send a note round to the Yard at eleven. The reply comes at midnight, in Lestrade's hand: a time, a room, and the words 'for God's sake bring your papers.'
options.requiresHint: Needs the Yard's trust

options.label: Go to the Streets. Wiggins's Boys, and No One Else.
options.detail: The road of shadow. It stays open if you chose it in February, or if you hired the boys since.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: We've got every back-door and cab-yard in the Professor's patch marked, Mr Holmes. All we want is the word.

options.outcome: Wiggins is on the doorstep within the hour, with his cap in his fist and eleven boys behind him in the area. You give the word. London has never looked so large, or so full of corners.
options.requiresHint: Needs the Irregulars

options.label: Put It in Your Brother's Hands.
options.detail: The road of power. It stays open if you chose it in February, or if your brother still trusts you.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: Come to the Club in the morning, Sherlock. Eleven o'clock. You will be received in the Strangers' Room. You will be expected to speak.

options.outcome: You send a single line to the Club by a street boy. The reply comes in four minutes, on a card of thick cream, in a hand like a row of well-drilled soldiers: 'Eleven. Do not be late. Do not bring Watson. M.'
options.requiresHint: Needs your brother's trust

options.label: Leave England. Take Watson Across the Channel Until the Net Is Drawn.
options.detail: The road of flight. It is always open, whatever you chose in February.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I have my bag. I have my revolver. I have an uncommonly low opinion of the British climate in any case. Where shall we be going?

options.outcome: You leave the house by the back, over the wall, as you came. At Victoria on Saturday morning there is a first-class carriage reserved in a name that is not yours. It is not a retreat, you tell yourself.

echoes.text: Watson has already packed a bag. He does not wait to be asked, and he does not pretend that he is not afraid.
A priest's black hangs on the door of the back bedroom, and there is a faint, rather holy smell of camphor.
A pea-jacket hangs on the door, and a beard lies on the washstand, looking dead.
A bowler sits on the hall table, and a clerk's coat hangs by it, with chalk on the cuffs.
At the corner of the street, a long coat and an odd-shaped stick that never touches the pavement. He is not there when you look again.

7B.title: A Death in Lombard Street
7B.description: Monday 16 March. The Times has it in four lines among the street accidents: a young man, a clerk, struck down by a runaway dray in Lombard Street at an early hour, and killed outright. The driver is not found. The inquest will sit on Thursday and will find, you are certain, that nobody is to blame. You read the paragraph three times. Then the door opens, and Mrs Hudson shows in a young woman in black, with a plain face and red eyes, who says that her brother is dead and that she has found your card in his coat.

options.label: Attend the Funeral and Hear What His Sister Has to Say.
options.detail: Do the human thing, and stand in the rain at Highgate. She knew more of his work than he ever told her.

quote.speaker: Miss Larch
quote.text: He said you were kind to him, Mr Holmes. He said it the last night. I should like to think it was true.

options.outcome: She has kept his letters, and in the letters are three addresses and the name of a coaching house. You are able to say, with some truth, that you were kind. It does not feel like a defence. But you walk away from Highgate with a sister's trust, and her brother's evidence.

options.label: Take Her Key to the Coaching House and Fetch the Ledger Tonight.
options.detail: His death should not be wasted. She has the key he was never meant to keep.

quote.speaker: Miss Larch
quote.text: It was in the lining of his hat. He said if anything happened, I was to give it to you and nobody else.

success.outcome: The key turns more softly than a picklock ever could. The ledger is behind the clock in the back room, as the dead man would have said. You are in Baker Street before the Professor's house has finished its supper, with the grey book in your coat and the sense of having stolen something from a grave.

failure.outcome: Someone has changed the lock since the funeral. The new one is stiff and loud, and a lamp comes up in the hall before the third turn. You run, and you are not quick enough to avoid being seen. By morning the Professor knows that the dead man's sister has been in his house.

options.label: Tell Yourself It Was a Necessary Price.
options.detail: A man died because you let him walk home. Grief will not mend that. Work might.

quote.speaker: Your own conscience
quote.text: You have made the same arithmetic before, and been right. That does not make it a pleasant sum.

options.outcome: You thank Miss Larch, give her what money you can spare, and see her to a cab. Then you turn back to the papers. It is a cold thing to do, and you do it well, and the hours pass more easily than you would have wished.

X1.title: The Slates of Vere Street
X1.description: Monday 9 February, three in the afternoon. The constable has let you up through a skylight on the understanding that you will not fall off. The roof is a long grey valley of slates and chimney-pots, and the rain of the morning has left it dark and shining. In the half-hour of daylight remaining you can learn one thing properly and the rest only by halves. There is a chalk mark scratched low on a chimney-stack. There is a heel-print in the soot beside the broken coping, the only mark on the roof that the rain has not touched. And there is the household of number nine, whose servants were at their windows when the brick fell.

options.label: Measure the Heel-Print in the Soot.
options.detail: A single clean mark, and the only one the rain has spared. It was made after the shower, by someone who knew you would pass.

quote.speaker: The constable
quote.text: Mind it, sir, don't tread on it. It's the only thing up here that looks like a man and not a pigeon.

options.outcome: You lay a sheet of paper on the soot and mark its edges with your pencil. The heel is worn hard on the outside, in the way of a man who spends his days sitting and his stops stamping, and the sole is wide and flat. He is not a thief by trade. He is a driver of some sort, and a heavy one, and he came up here in a hurry.

options.label: Examine the Chalk Mark on the Chimney.
options.detail: A sign of some kind, scratched with a stone. It might be a signal. It might be a child's idleness.

quote.speaker: The constable
quote.text: Boys, sir. They're up and down these roofs after pigeons all summer. I've a nephew chalks his name on everything.

options.outcome: You study it until the light begins to go. It is an ordinary scrawl, three strokes and a loop, made by a child with a bit of flint, a month old at least. You have spent a quarter of an hour on the sort of mark that a good detective is trained to be suspicious of, and a better one learns to ignore.

options.label: Question the Household at Number Nine.
options.detail: Servants see a great deal. They are also paid to tell you nothing.

quote.speaker: The housekeeper at number nine
quote.text: I saw nothing, sir, and I'll thank you not to say I did. I was at the copper, as I am every Monday, with my back to the window.

options.outcome: You are shown into a scullery that smells of soap and are given a cup of tea and more than a little civility. Nobody has seen anything. The housekeeper is anxious that you should not suppose that she has been looking out of windows, which tells you only that she has.

X2.title: The Mews Behind
X2.description: Monday, a little after four. Behind the houses there is a mews, a cobbled slot between two walls, with a coach-house at one end and a gate into the next street at the other. It is the only road a man could take off that roof without passing a window. The cobbles hold a good many things at this hour. There is a clay pipe lying by the drain, with a fresh-cut stem. There are two parallel ruts in the mud by the gate, narrow and deep. And a stable-boy sits on an upturned bucket with a ferret, regarding you with the carefully empty face of a boy who has been told not to talk to strangers.

options.label: Follow the Wheel-Ruts to the Gate.
options.detail: Two ruts, narrow and deep. A vehicle stood here, waiting, and was loaded to its springs.

quote.speaker: The stable-boy
quote.text: That's no dray, mister. A dray's wheels are wider than that. That's a hansom, and a heavy horse in it, and I know the horse.

options.outcome: The ruts run to the gate and turn into the street, where the traffic has erased them. But they are a cab's, not a dray's, and the near-side rut is deeper, as if one passenger had sat heavily on the left. At the kerb a few drops of lamp-oil lie in the road. A cab that stood here with its lamps lit by day was meant to be noticed by no one.

options.label: Test the Clay Pipe for Tobacco.
options.detail: A fresh stem and a filled bowl. It might tell you a man's brand, and his habits, and his purse.

quote.speaker: The stable-boy
quote.text: That's Mr Pritchard's pipe, mister. He's the coachman. He loses one a week. I find 'em in the drain and sell 'em back.

options.outcome: You turn it over in your glass. It is a common pipe, filled with a common shag, and it has never been lit. It was laid there tidily, in a place where it would be found and described, by a man who wished you to see a pipe-smoker. The boy, hearing this explained, gives it as his opinion that it was Mr Pritchard's all along.

options.label: Interview the Stable-Boy.
options.detail: He has been told to say nothing, which means he has been told that there is something to say.

quote.speaker: The stable-boy
quote.text: I never saw nobody, mister. And if I did, I never saw him, and if I saw him, he was a gentleman, and I never said so.

options.outcome: A sixpence moves him from silence to a long, circular account of everything that is not relevant, and in the middle of it a little hope: a gentleman did come through the mews on Friday, he says, a tall man in a plain coat who asked after nothing and looked at everything. You keep that. It is all the boy has.

X3.title: The Deduction at Baker Street
X3.description:
Monday, nine in the evening. The sitting-room is warm, and the lamp is lit, and the two traces of the afternoon lie on the table in front of you with all the other small things you have carried home. You have been told a hundred times, by clients and policemen and by Watson in his kindliest voice, that you do not explain yourself enough.

You explain yourself now, to the fire. A man on a roof, a man in a mews: the chain of them is short, and each link was forged by someone who did not know you were looking.

options.label: State the Whole Deduction: a Cabman From the Kentish Town Yard, Hired in Haste.
options.detail: The heel and the ruts, together. A driver of the heavier sort, a hansom waiting, and a single hired hand who never met his employer.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Fitch, you say, of a cab-yard in Kentish Town? I know that yard. I'd hoped never to hear it spoken of in connection with a gentleman.

options.outcome: You write the name on a card, and the address beneath it, and by ten o'clock it is on Lestrade's desk. The cab-yard in Kentish Town has been known to the Yard for years as a place where hansoms were hired out for odd work by odd men, and nobody had ever asked who paid. Now someone will. You have not caught the Professor. But you have, for the first time, a face at the end of one of his arms.
options.requiresHint: Needs both traces: the heel and the ruts

options.label: Venture a Partial Guess: a Driver of Some Kind.
options.detail: Say what you have, and no more. It will earn a little respect, and avoid a large embarrassment.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: A cabman, Holmes? Well, there are some four thousand cabmen in London. But I suppose it is a beginning.

options.outcome: You say that the man was a driver, and give the reasons. Watson nods, and writes it down, and admits that he would not have thought of it. It is a modest piece of work. It will be correct in the end, and it will be a month before anyone knows it.
options.requiresHint: Needs at least one of the two traces

options.label: Admit That You Cannot Yet Say.
options.detail: A confession that costs nothing, and teaches something. The best detective is the one who knows what he does not know.

quote.speaker: Mrs Hudson
quote.text: There, sir, I always say it's better to sleep on it. I put a cold chop out for you at seven. You never touched it.

options.outcome: You tell the fire that you have nothing, and the fire, which has heard it before, makes no comment. You eat the chop. You go to bed at ten. In the morning the thing is no clearer, but you are, and that is something.

4B.title: The Case Board
4B.description: Friday 20 February. You have declared war on the cleverest criminal in London, and in the eyes of the city you are still a consulting detective, and the notes go on arriving. Three of them stand on the mantelpiece against the clock tonight, tucked beneath the corner of a pipe-rack, in three hands. A scholar writes of a codex missing from a reading-room in Clerkenwell. A coachman's wife writes of a husband accused, who says he was in Kentish Town when it happened. A young woman signs herself only 'a governess in Hampstead' and writes that she is being followed. You have time for one, and you are not at all sure that you have time for any.

options.label: Take the Missing Codex.
options.detail: A tidy puzzle for a tidy mind, with a gentleman at the end of it who will be grateful. It will do your name no harm.

quote.speaker: The scholar
quote.text: It was there on Tuesday, Mr Holmes, and on Wednesday it was not. Nobody has left the building who was not searched. I cannot tell you how much it means to us.

options.outcome: You write to the scholar by the evening post and go to bed pleased with a small, clean problem.

options.label: Take the Coachman's Alibi.
options.detail: A humble client with a humbler purse. Kentish Town is not an address you have heard lightly of in the last six weeks.

quote.speaker: The coachman's wife
quote.text: He's a good man, sir, he never took so much as a penny. He says he was at the yard. And nobody there will say they saw him.

options.outcome: You do not tell her that the yard interests you. You tell her only that you will come in the morning.

options.label: Take the Governess in Hampstead.
options.detail: A young woman who is frightened and has nobody to tell. No fee, and no credit, and no reason to refuse.

quote.speaker: The governess
quote.text: I do not know who to go to, Mr Holmes. They say the police do not trouble themselves with letters. I only know that I am afraid to go out.

options.outcome: The paper is cheap, and the hand is steady, and the writer has taken the trouble to apologise three times for taking up your time. You answer by return.

options.label: Decline Them All and Sleep.
options.detail: A week of rest, at the price of three disappointed clients. Working against the Professor leaves no room for distraction. He also cannot afford to be exhausted.

quote.speaker: Mrs Hudson
quote.text: Nine hours, sir, if it's a minute. I looked in at noon and you were as dead to the world as a stone. I'll not say what I thought.

options.outcome: You write three polite refusals and go to bed. The clients take their troubles elsewhere, and you hear, a fortnight later, that the codex was found by a porter and the coachman acquitted by a jury and the governess driven from her post. It is hard to know what any of it would have cost. It is hard not to wonder.

K1.title: The Codex in the Reading-Room
K1.description: Monday 23 February. The Clerkenwell Institute's reading-room is a long, cold hall of green-shaded lamps, with a silence you could cut. The codex, a fourteenth-century book of hours with a binding of blue leather, was last seen on the table of a reader who has since gone home with a cold. The reader's slips, the porter's book and the binder's receipt are laid out in front of you by an anxious clerk. Everyone who entered was searched. Everyone who left was searched. The book, nevertheless, is not in the room.

options.label: Go Through the Readers' Slips Line by Line.
options.detail: Slow, dull and thorough. Somebody is lying, and the lie is on paper.

quote.speaker: The clerk
quote.text: Forty-one slips, Mr Holmes. I assure you they are all in order. I made out most of them myself.

options.outcome: In the forty-first slip the hand is the clerk's own, and the date is one day out. You say nothing. You ask for the binder's receipt, and the porter's book, and a cup of tea.

options.label: Follow the Binder's Receipt to His Shop.
options.detail: A book that leaves a room in a binder's parcel is not stolen. It is repaired.

quote.speaker: The porter
quote.text: The binder's boy comes on Wednesdays, sir, with a parcel under his arm. We never search the binder's boy. He's such a small thing.

options.outcome: The receipt gives an address in Hatton Wall. It is, you learn from the porter, the same hand that took the book in for repair the week before, and the same that returned it in a parcel on Wednesday. The binder's boy is the only person in London who is never searched.

options.label: Check the Pawnbrokers of Clerkenwell.
options.detail: A book is worth money only to someone. There are eleven shops that would know who.

quote.speaker: A pawnbroker
quote.text: A blue-leather book of hours, sir? No. But there was a gentleman asking, only yesterday, who would not give his name.

options.outcome: You visit nine shops in a long wet afternoon, and are offered a clock, a pair of boots and a stuffed owl. In the ninth a pawnbroker with a squint recalls a gentleman who made the same enquiry. The description is of the clerk.

K2.title: The Binder's Shop
K2.description: Tuesday 24 February. The binder works in a narrow, bookish house in Hatton Wall, where the stairs are lined with boards and the air tastes of paste. He is a nervous man with ink on his thumb and a daughter in the next room who plays the piano badly. When you put the question to him he does not look at you. He looks at the corner of the ceiling, as if the answer were written there.

options.label: Confront the Binder With the Clerk's Dated Slip.
options.detail: A blunt, bold stroke. If you have the order of events right, he will fall. If you have not, he will have a lawyer.

quote.speaker: The binder
quote.text: Sir, I never meant harm. The clerk said it was only to be gone a week. He said the Institute would be grateful for a better binding.

success.outcome: He gives way within a minute, and with him the whole little plot: a clerk in debt, a book lent to a collector, a binding to be 'improved'. The codex is recovered that afternoon, unharmed, from a drawer in Camden Town. The Institute's governors send a letter, and a cheque, and a large bunch of grapes.

failure.outcome: He has a better memory than you had hoped, and a better friend in Holborn. By evening a gentleman in a frock-coat has called to say that his client has been insulted. The codex reappears a week later on a doorstep, with no explanation, and the credit goes to someone else.

options.label: Recover the Book Quietly and Spare the Clerk.
options.detail: A man in debt is not the same as a thief. Offer the book's return without a scandal.

quote.speaker: The clerk
quote.text: I did not mean it for a theft, Mr Holmes. I meant to put it back on Sunday. I thought no one would ever know. I am so sorry.

options.outcome: The clerk is dismissed with a character, and the codex is back on its table by dawn. The governors thank you warmly and never ask for the details. You have done a small, kind thing, and the Yard, hearing of it, thinks a little better of you for it.

options.label: Hand the Whole Matter to Lestrade.
options.detail: A theft is a matter for the police. Let them take the credit, and the blame.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: You've brought me a tidy one, Mr Holmes. I'll not forget it. It's not often a gentleman hands over the arrest as well as the evidence.

options.outcome: Lestrade's constable arrives at six, and the binder and the clerk are in the cells by seven. The book is returned by midnight. Lestrade is in a good temper for a fortnight afterwards, and you find, to your faint surprise, that you are glad of it.

K3.title: The Coachman's Alibi
K3.description: Monday 23 February. The coachman's name is Dobbs, and he sits in a cell at Marylebone with his hat on his knees, a stout, sorrowful man of fifty who has driven a carriage for the same family for twenty years. He is accused of taking a silver snuff-box and a set of studs. He says he was in Kentish Town, at a livery yard, buying oats. Nobody at the yard remembers him. The yard's owner, he adds, was short with him, and told him that if he knew what was good for him he would forget the address.

options.label: Go to the Livery Yard in Kentish Town.
options.detail: A yard where a man is told to forget it is a yard worth looking at.

quote.speaker: The yard foreman
quote.text: We don't know any Dobbs. We don't know any oats, either. Move along, mister, you're blocking the gate.

options.outcome: The yard is long and bare and extremely clean, with twelve horses and eight cabs and a good many men who do not look like grooms. The foreman has the shoulders of a prize-fighter. In the corner stands a hansom with the near-side wheel freshly greased, and a heavy-set man in a driver's coat who looks, a little too quickly, the other way.

options.label: Question the Employer About the Missing Studs.
options.detail: A theft needs a thief and an owner. It is the owner who nearly always has something to hide.

quote.speaker: The employer
quote.text: I cannot say that I miss the snuff-box so very much, Mr Holmes. It is my wife who feels it. I should much prefer not to have a scene.

options.outcome: He is a pale, short-sighted man who has plainly never examined his own books. The studs, you learn, were pawned by a nephew in the autumn, and the snuff-box has been missing since a dinner in November. Nobody has been in the house who was not asked to be there. Dobbs is going to be acquitted in the end. The question is only whether he will be hanged by gossip first.

options.label: Look at the Coachman's Boots.
options.detail: A man tells you where he has been by what is on his feet.

quote.speaker: Dobbs
quote.text: I've not had them off since the arrest, sir. I'd sooner they didn't take my boots. They're the only good pair I've got.

options.outcome: The boots are stiff with a pale, fine-grained dust that is not found in Marylebone. It is a particular grey that you know, the dust of the lime-pits beyond Camden. It does not prove a word he has said, but it proves that he was not in the house where the studs were taken, and that is a start.

K4.title: The Alibi in the Yard
K4.description: Wednesday 25 February. You have a witness now, and a doubt, and a long, slow, uncomfortable idea. The Kentish Town yard is the same yard from which, you suspect, the man on the roof in Vere Street may have come. Dobbs is a harmless old man who has found himself on the edge of something. What you do next will free him, perhaps, and tell the yard that someone is looking.

options.label: Bring the Yard's Foreman Before a Magistrate to Swear to the Date.
options.detail: A public and lawful strike. It will free Dobbs and put the yard on notice, and burn a thread.

quote.speaker: The magistrate
quote.text: The accused is discharged. I should add that I find the evidence of the yard's foreman extremely curious, and I should be glad if the police would look into it.

options.outcome: Dobbs walks free, and the foreman, under oath, is forced to confirm that the old man was in his yard on the afternoon in question. It is a plain and unambiguous victory. It is also a public one, and by evening you know that the Professor's people have a new face to remember.

options.label: Let Wiggins's Boys Find Out Who Drives From the Yard.
options.detail: Do not break the case yet. Learn the yard, and free the coachman later.
options.outcome: For ten days the boys sit on the wall opposite, with a nail-bag and a tray of matches, and write down every wheel. You learn the name of three drivers and the colour of one dog-cart. Dobbs stays in his cell a fortnight longer, and writes you a letter that is polite and hard to read.

options.label: Pay the Coachman's Bail and Leave the Yard Alone.
options.detail: A kind and cautious answer. Dobbs goes home, and the yard never knows.

quote.speaker: Dobbs
quote.text: You're a gentleman, sir. I'll not forget it. If ever you want a carriage driven, there's not a man in London can take a corner as I can.

options.outcome: You put down the five pounds at the desk and are given a receipt in triplicate. Dobbs walks out into the rain, grey and bewildered and grateful, and shakes your hand with both of his. The yard in Kentish Town goes on as before.

K5.title: The Governess in Hampstead
K5.description: Monday 23 February. Miss Adelaide Crewe is twenty-three, plain, neat and rather thin, and she sits on the edge of your sofa with her hands folded in her lap as if she had been told not to touch anything. She has been the governess in a respectable house in Hampstead for eighteen months. Three weeks ago the first letter came: unsigned, printed in a neat type, and civil. It said that she had a secret. It did not say what. Since then there have been seven letters, and a man at the gate who vanishes when she looks, and she has begun to be afraid of the post.

options.label: Read the Letters Closely and Trace the Printer.
options.detail: Printed type has a hand as plain as writing. This one was set by a man who is good at it.

quote.speaker: Miss Crewe
quote.text: It is not that they say anything dreadful, Mr Holmes. It is that they are so polite. Each one begins 'Dear Madam' and ends 'your well-wisher'.

options.outcome: The type is a good, fresh Caslon, set by a master hand, and there is a flaw in the lower-case 'g' that you recognise from three other documents in your files. The printer is in Clerkenwell. You do not yet know why a printer of his skill should trouble himself with a governess.

options.label: Watch the House in Hampstead for the Man at the Gate.
options.detail: A patient evening in the cold. If he comes, you will see him, and he will not see you.

quote.speaker: The gardener
quote.text: There's a man been at that gate since Wednesday, sir, a lean, quiet sort, with a stick. I'd have sent him off, only he's so polite about it.

options.outcome: He is a thin, grave, brown-faced man in a long coat, with an odd-shaped stick under his arm, and he stands beneath the gate-lamp for forty minutes, looking at the third-floor window. At nine he goes, and you follow, and lose him in Heath Street. It is a name you will hear again.

options.label: Ask Watson to Call and Hear Her Story as a Doctor.
options.detail: A frightened young woman, and a physician's kindly manner. It may bring out what a detective cannot.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: She is not hysterical, Holmes. She is frightened, and sensible, and she has not slept in a fortnight. I should say she is telling every word of the truth.

options.outcome: Watson takes her tea and her pulse and her story, in that order. He comes away with a clearer account than you could have wrung from her in a week, and a look of cold fury you have not seen since the Sholto case. 'Someone,' he says, 'is going to answer for this.'

K6.title: What the Letters Wanted
K6.description: Wednesday 25 February. The letters, you find, were never meant to be read as a threat. They were a lever. Miss Crewe's employer, a banker in Hampstead, has been quietly asked by a gentleman of the City to hold certain accounts. A governess's reputation is an excellent thing to hold over a man who might one day wish to refuse. It is petty, cold, and exactly in the Professor's manner. And Miss Crewe is the one who is being used to do it.

options.label: Protect Her Openly and Tell the Banker What Is Being Done.
options.detail: A direct, honest thing to do. It will cost you a quarrel and save a young woman's peace.

quote.speaker: Miss Crewe
quote.text: You did not have to do this, Mr Holmes. I could not pay you. I should like to say that I shall not forget it, and I hope that I shall have the chance to prove it.

options.outcome: The banker goes white, and then red, and then, to your surprise, gentlemanly indeed. Miss Crewe keeps her post, and the letters cease. You have made an enemy of a man who wished to be bought, and a friend of a young woman who was being used. It is, you think, a better exchange than most.

options.label: Use Her as Bait for the Clerkenwell Printer.
options.detail: A girl who has been sent letters is a girl whom the sender will watch. If you watch the watcher, you learn the printer.

quote.speaker: Miss Crewe
quote.text: You want me to carry on as if I did not know, Mr Holmes? I am afraid. But if it will help, I will do it. You have been kind.

options.outcome: She does it bravely, and badly, and for nine days. On the tenth you take the printer's courier on the Heath with a bundle of letters under his arm, and the whole sorry apparatus is laid open. She never complains. When it is over she resigns her post, and goes to her sister's in the north, and does not write. You are not sorry for what you have learned. You are not sure that you are sorry enough.

options.label: Send Her to Watson's Wife and Close the Matter.
options.detail: A safe house and a quiet fortnight. Let her be a guest and not a pawn, and the letters will stop of themselves.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Mary will be delighted. She has been wanting someone to teach her German verbs for six months. You have done a decent thing, Holmes. I shall say so, and be damned.

options.outcome: Miss Crewe spends a fortnight in Kensington, drinks a great deal of tea, and is taught to play whist. By the end of it the letters have stopped, since there is no longer anybody for them to find. You have lost a thread, and Watson has gained a friend. It was, on the whole, worth it.

5B.title: The Boys' First Report
5B.description: Monday 9 March. Wiggins comes at eight, in a clean collar, with a notebook of his own, and reads out the first week's work as though he were giving evidence at the Old Bailey. The boys have been everywhere. They have watched the Professor's house, the coaching establishment and the three cab-yards. They have followed a black horse in a dog-cart with yellow wheels for four days and lost it three times. They have, he says, a long list of public-houses. And two of the boys have been sick from eating a pie, which he thinks you ought to know.

options.label: Follow the Black Horse and the Yellow Wheels.
options.detail: The one thing that is theirs and only theirs. A dog-cart that never takes a fare is a dog-cart with something to hide.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: He goes out at one in the morning, Mr Holmes, and he's never back till four. And there's a man in the back who never gets out and never speaks.

success.outcome: The dog-cart is found by the boys, and followed by you, to a house in Camden Town with a green door. It stands there for an hour with its lamps shaded. When it leaves, a short man in a brown coat goes in, and does not come out. You have, for the first time, a house to watch, and a man to look for.

failure.outcome: You follow it down three streets and lose it at a crossing. The driver, who has not once looked round, raises his whip as he goes, in a salute that is gentle indeed. It is a courtesy, and a warning. He knew he was followed from the start.

options.label: Send Two Boys to Every Public-House on the List.
options.detail: Twenty-two houses and forty-four boys' worth of dull listening. Talk in a taproom may be overheard.
options.outcome: For eight days the taverns of London are infested with small, solemn children who look, to the landlords, as though they are waiting for their fathers. You get a list of names, a map of twenty-two houses, and a bill. In a snug at Limehouse a boy hears two men discuss a Monday, and a Colonel, and a large sum.

options.label: Give Them a Week's Rest. They Are Children.
options.detail: Two of them have been sick. They are tired, and thin, and have been out in all weathers. Let them be boys for a week.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: Rest, Mr Holmes? We never had that offered before. I don't think I know what to do with it. I'll tell them. They'll think I've gone soft.

options.outcome: Wiggins stares at you for a long moment, as if looking for the catch. When he finds there is none he puts his cap back on, slowly, and says that he will tell the boys. They spend the week in a field at Hendon, throwing stones at a bottle. You have not spent money better this year. You can feel it, a little, in the way Wiggins stands when he returns.

7D.title: The Divisional Book
7D.description: Friday 20 March. The Marylebone divisional book is a huge ledger kept under a green baize cloth, and your name is in it, in a clerk's round hand: 'Entry by night, rear premises, coaching establishment, Marylebone Road. Persons unknown. Description of one: tall, lean, dark.' Superintendent Hallam, who has never in his life been rude to anybody, sits across from you in his office with the book open between you and does not ask whether the description is accurate. He asks, with painful politeness, whether you would like a cup of tea.

options.label: Own Up and Offer to Make Good.
options.detail: An honest confession, in a quiet room. It will cost you a little pride and a great deal of face. It may also be remembered.

quote.speaker: Superintendent Hallam
quote.text: I'm obliged to you, Mr Holmes. It's a rare gentleman who walks into a police station to say he's broken into somebody's house. I'd as soon not charge you if I could help it. Could I help it?

options.outcome: You tell the whole thing, plainly and without excuse. Hallam listens, writes nothing down, and in the end tears a small sheet from the ledger and puts it in the fire. 'I never saw you,' he says. 'And I'll thank you never to do it again.' You walk out into Marylebone High Street with the odd, light feeling of having put down a small, shameful thing.

options.label: Ask Lestrade to Have the Entry Quashed.
options.detail: A word from the Yard to the division. It will cost Lestrade a favour, and you the right to ask for another.
options.outcome: The entry disappears from the divisional book within the week, and the Superintendent forgets your name. Lestrade says nothing about it. But he is a little colder at the Yard next time, and his handshake, when it comes, is a shade less warm. A favour like that is a coin that does not come back.
options.requiresHint: Needs Lestrade's trust

options.label: Deny Everything and Keep to Your Rooms.
options.detail: Deny, and wait. A description is not a conviction.

quote.speaker: Superintendent Hallam
quote.text: You have been in your rooms the whole of the night in question, Mr Holmes? Quite so. Mrs Hudson will say the same, I dare say. A landlady is always so reliable.

success.outcome: Hallam closes the book and says, dutifully, that there is evidently some mistake. You are shown out with a bow. It is a hollow victory, but a victory.

failure.outcome: The Superintendent has been talking to the tutor in the dressing-gown, who is positive about your coat. By the evening the whole division knows. The Yard hears of it by the morning. You are a gentleman of reputation who has lied to a policeman, and the lie is worth more to your enemies than the burglary.

9B.title: The Dead Man Walks
9B.description: Wednesday 15 April. For five days you have been a notice in the Standard, a wreath from the Yard, and a subject of conversation in every public-house between Baker Street and Whitehall. Mrs Hudson has been weeping in the kitchen, and a good many people have remembered, in print, how clever you were. It has not been entirely agreeable to read. Now there is a knock at the door, and then a second, firmer one, and the unmistakable tread of a man with a stick and an upset stomach. It is Watson.

options.label: Show Yourself to Watson and Tell Him at Once.
options.detail: He has grieved for five days. It is not a kindness to extend it.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Holmes. I shall sit down, if you will forgive me, before I fall. And then I shall decide whether to embrace you or to strike you.

options.outcome: He decides on both, in that order, and then has a glass of brandy, and then another. When he has recovered he asks, with great dignity, whether you had any particular reason for not telling him. You say that you did. He says that he hopes it was a good one. It was, but you are aware, as he says it, that it was not good enough.

options.label: Keep Up the Pretence a Few Days Longer.
options.detail: The trick is working. The Professor's men are slack. A week of it may be worth a month of watching.

quote.speaker: Mrs Hudson
quote.text: I've never been so ashamed in my life, sir, to see that poor gentleman sit in that chair and cry. And you in the next room all the while with your hand over your mouth.

options.outcome: You keep the pretence a further four days, in the back bedroom, with the blinds down. The yield is large: a dozen small observations on the Professor's men, each worth a week's labour. The cost is paid at the end, in Watson's face. He does not reproach you. He only says that he did not think that you could do it, and then he says that he sees that you could.

options.label: Send for Lestrade and Reveal It to the Yard.
options.detail: A man who has been officially mourned owes the force an official resurrection. It will do your Standing good.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Well, I'm blessed. And here was I having a collection taken up for a stone. The lads will want their shilling back.

options.outcome: Lestrade arrives within the hour and sits for a long moment on the edge of the sofa, looking at you with an expression that is not quite anger and not quite relief. When he speaks he is gruff. The Yard, he says, has been good about the wreath. You say that you will pay for it. He says that you had better.

F1.title: The First Move
F1.description: Saturday 14 February. You have a name, a brick that did not hit you, and a spring before you in which a man who has never once been charged with anything intends to go on being so. It is not enough to fight him alone, and it is much too late to fight him in the dark. There are four doors in London that will open to you tonight. Each leads somewhere you cannot easily come back from, and each of them wants something in return. The Yard wants you to be believed. The street wants you to be ruthless, and kind. Whitehall wants you to be obedient. And the fourth door is the one you open yourself, and it leads out of England.

options.label: Take It to Scotland Yard.
options.detail: The law, slowly: files, warrants and a Chief Inspector's patience. The road of proof, which asks you to be believed.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: You'll want to come in on Tuesday, Mr Holmes. Bring whatever you've got, and bring it in order. I'll see you get the Chief for twenty minutes. I can't promise more.

options.outcome: You send a note round to the Yard, and the answer comes back in the hour: a time, a room, and a line that says 'for pity's sake, bring your papers'. Nobody has said they would listen since January.

options.label: Send for Wiggins and the Boys.
options.detail: The street: twelve pairs of eyes, a shilling a day, and nobody to answer to. The road of shadow, which asks you to be ruthless, and kind.
options.outcome: A street boy takes the message at a run, and by nightfall there is a small, grave, ink-stained face at the area door, with its cap in its hand. The boys do not ask what it is for. They only ask when they start.

options.label: Call at Your Brother's Club.
options.detail: Whitehall: the machinery of the State, and a price, and the one man in England who has never been surprised. The road of power, which asks you to be obedient.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: I have been wondering, Sherlock, how long it would be before you came. I had thought the end of the month. It is a mark of how well I know you that I have laid a second place.

options.outcome: The Diogenes Club has not a single sound in it, as usual, but the hall porter, who has never smiled, takes your hat and says that Mr Mycroft is expecting you in the Strangers' Room. He says it as one who has been told to say it for several days.

options.label: Trust No One. Work It Alone, and Keep the Road Out of England Open.
options.detail: The long way round: your own papers, your own legs and, at the end of it, a train. The road of flight, which asks you to be alone.
options.outcome: You draw the curtains and turn the key, and for a long moment there is no sound in the room but the clock. It is, you think, exactly how you would have wished it to be, and for the first time that has the sound of a complaint.

MA.title: A Word at the Diogenes Club
MA.description: Tuesday 17 February. The Strangers' Room has not changed in the three years since you were last in it. It has the same long table, the same unlit fire in the same cold grate. The same vast, unhurried, flannel-clad shape at the head of the table, with its hands folded across its waistcoat like a pair of sleeping cats. Mycroft listens to the whole of your account with his eyes shut. When it is done he opens them and says that he knows of the Professor, and has known for six years, and has never yet been asked what to do about him.

options.label: Accept an Introduction to Superintendent Greaves of Special Branch.
options.detail: A silent, courteous man with thirty silent, courteous men. He will not ask why. He will not tell you what he knows, either.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: Greaves has watched the Professor's people for six years, Sherlock, and has not once been permitted to touch them. He will be extremely glad to be asked. He will conceal it perfectly.

options.outcome: Mycroft writes four words on a Club card, blots it with the ceremony of a man signing a treaty, and hands it across. It says only 'You may trust him. M.' You have never in your life seen your brother so brief, or so exact.

options.label: Take Information Only, Not Men.
options.detail: Whatever Whitehall knows, and nobody to answer to. Quiet, independent, and a good deal less than you might have had.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You are afraid of obligation, Sherlock. It has always been your fault, and it is, I confess, the quality I most envy in you. You shall have what I know. You shall not have to thank me for it.
