The compartment is empty but for one other passenger, a stout, pleasant, red-faced German in a green hat who has been looking out of the window for the better part of an hour, and who has, in that time, not once turned a page of his newspaper. He is a good traveller. He is also holding the paper upside down.

options.label: Talk to Him in German and Learn What You Can.
options.detail: A quiet remark, a pleasant face. Let him think you a harmless Englishman, and listen to what he does not say.

quote.speaker: The German in the green hat
quote.text: You are English, mein Herr? I have a cousin in Manchester. A large place. They tell me nobody there ever speaks to anybody.

success.outcome: You discuss his cousin, the price of tobacco and the beauties of the Black Forest for forty minutes, and in the course of it he lets fall the name of a hotel in Meiringen that nobody in Basel has any reason to have heard. He gets out at the next station with a perfectly easy smile. You have not caught him. But you know where his master is sending the others.

failure.outcome: He is a good deal cleverer than he looks. Within ten minutes it is he who is asking the questions, so pleasantly that you hardly notice, and in the end you have told him a great many small things about yourself and learned almost nothing about him. He gets out at the next station and tips his green hat to Watson, who is still asleep.

options.label: Wake Watson and Have Him Feign an Attack of Faintness.
options.detail: A doctor has authority. A stranger will give up a seat to a sick man, and the compartment to the man's physician.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You wish me to be ill, Holmes? On a railway train, in front of a foreigner? I have never in my life done anything so undignified. Move your feet, I shall want to lie down.

options.outcome: Watson is magnificent. He sways, he groans, he calls for a window to be opened, and at the end of five minutes the German is on the platform at Mulhouse with a handkerchief to his face, saying something about a connection. 'I trust,' says Watson, sitting up and straightening his hat, 'that I shall never be asked to do that again.' He looks, you think, pleased.
options.requiresHint: Needs Watson's trust

options.label: Show Him the Pistol in Your Coat and Say Nothing.
options.detail: No words, no argument. A man in a green hat who has seen a revolver in an English coat will usually find that he has urgent business elsewhere.

quote.speaker: The German in the green hat
quote.text: Ach. I see I have been rude, mein Herr. A man ought not to stare. I shall go and sit with the other gentlemen. It is much more cheerful.

options.outcome: He goes at once, with a polite bow, and a smile which is a little too fixed. You sit for the rest of the journey with your hand in your pocket and your eyes on the door. It is a crude solution.

echoes.text: The black soutane is at the bottom of your trunk, and you wonder, with a certain grim humour, whether a priest would have been asked any questions at all.

C6B.title: The Steamer on the Lake of Thun
C6B.description:
Saturday 2 May. The little steamer goes up the lake in the thin spring sunshine, with a ripple of white at her bow and a smell of coal-smoke and fresh water. The snow-peaks stand about the lake like a company of old men at a funeral, and the passengers lean on the rail and say 'ach' and 'oh' and 'ravishing'.

For two hours, for the first time since January, nobody is following you. Watson sits on a coil of rope, with his hat tilted over his eyes, and says nothing, and it is the best thing that has happened in three months.

options.label: Tell Him What You Intend if It Comes to the End.
options.detail: A man should not walk into the mountains without a word. If the worst happens, he will want to know that you had a plan.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I see. You think it will end at the water. You will not say so, of course, but you think it. Well. I do not accept it, Holmes. But I thank you for telling me.

options.outcome: You tell him quietly, in the lee of the funnel, that if it comes to the worst there will be a note, and where to look for it. He does not interrupt. When you have finished he puts his hand over yours on the rail, and holds it there for a minute, and says nothing at all. The lake is perfectly beautiful, and neither of you looks at it.

options.label: Ask After Mary, and the Practice, and Let Him Talk.
options.detail: He has put his whole life aside to follow you. Give him an hour of it back.
options.outcome: He talks for an hour about his wife, and the practice, and the dreadful state of the roof in Kensington, and the new curate who preaches on the subject of drains. You listen with real attention. It is not what you would have chosen to listen to a year ago. It is, you find, extremely restful.

options.label: Watch the Other Passengers for a Face You Know.
options.detail: A lake steamer is a small stage. If the Colonel is on it, you will see him.

quote.speaker: A Swiss purser
quote.text: You are looking for somebody, monsieur? I have a good memory for faces. I shall tell you at once that I have seen nobody who is not a tourist or a priest.

success.outcome: You find him at the stern, a tall, lean, sunburnt Englishman in a long coat, with a violin-case under his arm and a book that he is not reading. He does not look at you. He gets off at Spiez, without looking back. You tell Watson nothing. But you watch the shore until the steamer is out of sight of it.

failure.outcome: You see a Colonel in every shadow, and a Professor in every hat, and by the end of the voyage you have frightened a Swiss schoolmaster, a Dutch bride and a large, surprised Bishop. Watson takes you by the arm and leads you to a bench. 'You will sit down,' he says kindly, 'and you will look at the mountains.'

C7B.title: The Guide's Warning
C7B.description:
Sunday 3 May, in the dusk. The proprietor of the inn at Meiringen has sent for a guide, a leathery old Swiss named Hans who has spent his life on those paths and who talks to you in a slow and patient English like a man reading from an old book.

The path to the Falls, he says, is closed at nightfall, by custom and by common sense. It is cut into the rock, and the spray freezes on it by dark. A man might slip and nobody know. Also, he adds, in the same slow voice, a tall Englishman with a violin-case has asked him the way to the Falls three times today.

options.label: Walk the Path With Him at Dusk and Learn the Ledge.
options.detail: If it comes to a struggle on that rock, the man who knows every foot of it has the advantage. It is a chilly evening's work.

quote.speaker: Hans, the guide
quote.text: Here you put your foot, sir, and here you do not. There is a ledge below, and a crack, and a second ledge below that. I have seen a goat go down it. I have never seen a man.

options.outcome: You walk the whole path in the last of the light, with the roar of the water growing in your ears and the spray cold on your face. Hans points out each place with his stick: the ledge, the crack, the second ledge below. You look at each of them for a long time. You do not say why. He does not ask.

options.label: Send a Coded Telegram to Mycroft.
options.detail: A short message, saying only where you are. He will know what to do with it, and he will not be pleased to be woken.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: Received. Moriarty left Paris on Friday for Geneva. He will be in Meiringen by Monday. I regret that I can do nothing more at this distance. Be careful, and do not do anything noble. M.

options.outcome: The reply comes within the hour, which is, for Mycroft, the speed of an alarm bell. It tells you in nineteen words what you had half-guessed in four days. You tear it up and put the pieces in the stove, and sit looking at the glow. 'Do not do anything noble.' It is the most affectionate thing he has ever said to you.

options.label: Rest. You Will Need Every Ounce of It Tomorrow.
options.detail: A man who goes to a struggle already tired has half lost it. You have not slept properly since Geneva.
options.outcome: You sleep for nine hours with Watson in the chair by the window, and when you wake it is bright morning and the smell of coffee is rising up the stair. For ten minutes you lie quite still, looking at the beams of the ceiling, and you do not think about anything at all.

options.label: Hire a Second Guide to Follow the Englishman.
options.detail: A pair of eyes on the stranger, at a franc an hour. It costs a little. It tells you where he sleeps.

quote.speaker: Hans, the guide
quote.text: My nephew is a good boy, sir, and quiet on his feet. He will follow the gentleman and say nothing, and he will tell you in the morning where the gentleman has slept.

options.outcome: By midnight you know that the tall Englishman has taken a room at the other inn, that he has not undressed, and that he has been out twice to look at the path by lantern. He sits in his window with the lamp turned down. You cannot see his face. But you know the shape of the stick.

options.label: Look Up the Lady Who Has Taken the Room Below Yours.
options.detail: She registered on Friday, in a name that is not hers, and has not been out of the house since. It is exactly the kind of room that she would take.

quote.speaker: The proprietor
quote.text: A lady in grey, Monsieur? Yes, on the first floor, but she says she will not be disturbed. She is a lady of the most extraordinary firmness.

options.outcome: You go down the stair in the dusk, and she is already standing at her door, with a lamp.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs to have met Mrs Norton

H1.title: A Cup of Coffee in Florence
H1.description:
Wednesday 6 May 1891. The cafe is in a quiet street behind the Duomo, with a green awning and four small tables. You have been sitting at one of them for an hour with an English newspaper three days old and a bandage under your glove.

It says that you are dead. It says it in a long and handsome obituary, in a black border, with a good many adjectives, and a paragraph on the Professor, who is also said to be dead, and a paragraph on the Falls. You read it twice. There is a great deal in it that is true. It is strange to be mourned so well.

options.label: Tell No One. Let the World Think It True.
options.detail: A man who is dead is hard to hunt. Every friend you tell is a friend who might be made to speak.

quote.speaker: Your own conscience
quote.text: It is a sound plan, and it is the loneliest that I can think of. I should be sorry to see you carry it out. I should be a good deal sorrier to see you break it.

options.outcome: You fold the paper and put it in your pocket. You pay for the coffee, in francs, and go out into the sun with a new name, which is not yet quite your own, and a passport that is entirely your own and entirely false. Nobody in Florence turns to look.

options.label: Write to Your Brother, and to Him Alone.
options.detail: Mycroft keeps secrets as a cellar keeps wine. He will send money, and he will tell no one. It is a measured sort of trust.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: I have put on mourning, Sherlock. It is becoming, I am told. I shall send what you ask. I shall say nothing to anyone. I confess I had begun to fear that I should be wearing the black in earnest.

options.outcome: You write four lines in the cipher your family used as boys, and post them in a letter-box in the Via Tornabuoni. Eleven days later a draft arrives at a bank in Florence, in a name you have never used, and a note: 'Do not come home yet.' You laugh, aloud, in the street, for the first time in a month.

options.label: Write to Watson and Risk the Colonel Seeing It.
options.detail: He has been sitting in a dark room, mourning you. A single line would give him back the world. It might also give the Colonel your address.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I have your note, Holmes. I should only like you to know that I have never in my life been so glad of a piece of paper.

success.outcome: The letter goes by a Swiss courier and a Parisian bookseller and a Dutch widow who owes Mycroft a favour. It reaches Watson in Kensington on the eleventh day, in a plain envelope, in an unfamiliar hand. He reads it standing up, and puts it into the fire, and then, in a quiet voice, tells his wife that he will be needing a little extra sleep.

failure.outcome: The letter is opened at a sorting-house in Dover by a clerk who has been paid very well to open a particular kind of envelope. Within three days a tall, lean, sunburnt man is standing outside a cafe in Florence, looking at the awning. You have gone by then. But you know that you have been found, and that he is a patient man.

H2.title: The Norwegian Explorer
H2.description: Spring 1892. The monastery stands on a spur of rock above a valley that has never been described in English, and the lamas who live in it have never seen a Norwegian, which is exactly what you have decided to be. The air is thin and cold, and clear, and nothing has happened here for four hundred years. In the morning you walk on the terrace in a sheepskin coat with a notebook, and in the afternoon you sit in a cold cell with an old monk who is teaching you to be quiet. It is not an art that you have ever practised.

options.label: Study With the Lamas and Learn to Sit Still.
options.detail: A man who can do nothing for an hour can do a great deal more than he could. It is a hard school.

quote.speaker: The old lama
quote.text: You think too much, Sigerson. It is a fault. In this country we call it a disease, and treat it with butter-tea and silence.

options.outcome: For ten months you sit in the cold, and drink butter-tea, and say nothing at all. The old man corrects your posture with a stick. By the spring you can sit for four hours without moving a muscle, and your mind, for the first time since you were a boy, is as still as a pond.

options.label: Send the Foreign Office a Report on the Passes.
options.detail: A traveller sees what a map does not. Your brother would value it, and it would repay the money he has sent.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: Your report on the Himalayan passes has been read by three departments and a minister. They are most anxious to know who 'Sigerson' is. I have told them that he is a Norwegian, and that they are not to enquire further.

options.outcome: You spend the summer in the saddle, with a compass and a notebook, and send back a long, exact account of the passes and the garrisons. It is read with attention. In London a senior man in a quiet room says that it is the best thing of its kind he has seen. Your name is not on it. Your brother does not tell you what it is worth. You are proud.

options.label: Keep to Yourself and Let the Years Pass.
options.detail: You came here to disappear. A man who disappears does not make friends, or notes.

quote.speaker: The old lama
quote.text: You are polite, Sigerson, and you say nothing. It is a good way to be a ghost. I would not recommend it to anyone I liked.

options.outcome: You keep your cell, your notebook and your own counsel. The monks leave you alone, with the vague, kindly tact of men who have seen a great many people come here to be left alone. When you go down the valley at the end of the year, you realise that you have not said a hundred words aloud since the spring.

echoes.text: A thin, brown-faced Englishman was seen at the foot of the pass in March, asking the way to a Norwegian. He was turned back by the snow. He will not be turned back twice.
At the foot of the pass, in the dusk, a mule driver says that a tall Englishman asked him the way to a Norwegian. He gave a wrong answer, he says, out of habit.

H3.title: The Coal-Tar Laboratory
H3.description: 1893. The laboratory at Montpellier is a long white room with a high ceiling and a row of north windows, and it smells of benzene, hot glass and good cigars. You have been at work there for eight months on the derivatives of coal-tar, under a name that nobody has asked about. It is, you suppose, the happiest period of your life, and you are aware of it as one is aware of a held breath. A letter reaches you in the autumn, forwarded by your brother, in his hand, with four lines. A grievous loss has fallen on Watson. He is not well. He is very much alone.

options.label: Go to Him at Once, Whatever It Costs.
options.detail: A friend in grief cannot be waited for. The Colonel is still at large, and a man who goes home goes home to danger.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I had thought, Holmes, that I should never again hear that step on the stair. I find that I was mistaken in at least one particular.

options.outcome: You are in London in thirty-one hours, in a closed cab, in the dark. You sit with him in a silent room until morning, and say very little, and it is, perhaps, the only thing you have ever done that you are wholly sure of. The Colonel does not know. Mycroft, informed by telegram, says only that you are a fool and that he is glad of it.

options.label: Write Through Your Brother and Stay at Your Work.
options.detail: A letter is a gentle thing, and it can be carried by a man who has no secret to keep. It is not the same as a presence. It is better than nothing.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: I shall carry your letter myself. I shall say that it is from a distant friend, a person of great consideration. I do not think he will be deceived. But I think he will be comforted.

options.outcome: Your brother carries the letter, with a face like a funeral, and puts it on Watson's table without a word. Watson reads it twice. He asks who sent it. Your brother says that he cannot say. Watson says, quietly, that he thought so, and folds the paper, and asks whether Mycroft would like some tea.

options.label: Stay. You Cannot Be Seen, and the Work Is Nearly Done.
options.detail: Coming out of hiding too soon undoes everything that hiding has done. It is a cold sum, and an accurate one.

quote.speaker: Your own conscience
quote.text: You have always preferred the sum to the answer, and the answer to the man. It has been a long time since I thought it a virtue.

options.outcome: You stay, and you work, and in the spring the monograph is finished. It is a good piece of research, and it will never carry your name. You have it bound in morocco and put on a shelf. When you look at it, there is, in the corner of your mind, a small, bright, accusing light.

echoes.text: You do not know whether he has the letter you sent from Florence, or whether it was one of the many things that go astray. You only know that a man who has been written to does not grieve in quite the same way.

H4.title: The Return
H4.description:
April 1894. The news comes by a London paper two days old, in a cafe in Montpellier: a young gentleman of fashion has been shot dead in a locked room in Park Lane, with a pistol-bullet that nobody can explain. The Yard is baffled.

It is, you think, exactly the sort of case that you would have wanted. And you have just learned, from a short note in your brother's hand, that of all the men who ever wished you harm, only one is left alive and at large in London. It is time to decide whether Sherlock Holmes is dead.

options.label: Come Back to Baker Street in a Wig and Spectacles, and Show Yourself to Watson in His Own Study.
options.detail: A theatrical entrance, perhaps. He has had three years of quiet. It may be kinder to be abrupt than to be slow.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I think, Holmes, that I am going to be extremely ill. I should be obliged if you would simply stand there for a moment, and let me look.

success.outcome: You walk into his study in the dress of an old bookseller with a bag of volumes on his arm, and set them on the table, and say that you are sorry to have startled him. He faints, dead away, and falls, with great exactness, into the chair. When he comes round he is crying, and you are on your knees with the brandy. 'You always had a theatrical streak,' he says, and cannot stop laughing.

failure.outcome: It goes wrong at once. The old bookseller's bag falls open, and the volumes scatter, and Watson, who has been up all night, mistakes you for a burglar and has his service revolver out before the second book hits the carpet. You are a long minute explaining who you are, and for the first time in his life Watson is not in the least pleased. It is a long time before you are forgiven.

options.label: Have Mycroft Prepare the Ground, and Return Quietly.
options.detail: A letter first, a visit after, and a cold supper laid in the old rooms. It is a gentle road, and it is slow.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: I have kept the rooms exactly as they were, Sherlock. Mrs Hudson has dusted them every Thursday, and has never once asked why a man who is dead should have his pipes kept filled. She is a remarkable woman.

options.outcome: Mycroft sends a short note to Kensington, which says that a visitor is expected and that the visitor is not to be alarmed. You come in the evening, with your own key, to the old sitting-room. The lamp is lit, and the fire is made, and a cold supper laid for two. Watson, in the armchair, does not turn round. 'Well,' he says, in a steady voice, 'you took your time.'

options.label: Stay Sigerson. Let the Dead Stay Dead.
options.detail: You have another name, another trade, and a long and peaceful life in front of you. There is not a soul in London who will blame you.
options.outcome: You put the Park Lane paper down on the table, and finish your coffee, and ask the waiter for the bill. A week later you are in a small house in the south, with a chemical bench and a window on a garden. London has its mystery, and the Yard its bafflement. Somebody else will solve it, in the end, or no one will. You do not read the papers.

echoes.text: You have been to London once already, in the dark, and sat in a silent room until morning. Nobody knows it but Watson, and he has been careful never to say.

M1.title: The Strangers' Room
M1.description: Saturday 25 April, eleven in the morning. The Diogenes Club is the only place in London where nobody speaks, and the one room in it where talking is permitted is on the first floor, at the back, with the blinds half down. It has a long table, six chairs, a fire that is never allowed to go out, and, tonight, three men. Mycroft sits at the head, vast and unhurried. On his right is the Permanent Secretary of the Home Office, a thin grey man named Aldous. On his left is a man from the Treasury, who has been introduced by his initials. They have been listening to you for twenty minutes. Mycroft has not once looked at the clock.

options.label: Accept the Government's Terms Entire.
options.detail: The machinery of the State at your elbow: Special Branch, the Bank, the Telegraph. In return, whatever you find belongs to the Crown, and goes where the Crown says.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You will find it a great convenience, Sherlock, to have the State at your back. You will also find that it does not like to be asked what it intends. I think you will learn to be content with that.

options.outcome: Aldous makes a note. The man from the Treasury makes a second one. Mycroft folds his hands over his waistcoat and says that the papers will be drawn up by Monday and that in the meantime you may consider yourself a person of consequence. It is a comfortable feeling. You notice, as you go down the stairs, that your hand has gone to your pocket, as if to make sure that it is still yours.

options.label: Accept, With One Condition: the Law Is Allowed to Run.
options.detail: Use the State's tools, but let the courts have what the courts can use. A reservation, quietly stated, and possibly resented.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: A condition, Sherlock? From you? I had expected something much more extravagant. Very well. Mr Aldous will write it down in a form that allows us all to disregard it at our leisure.

options.outcome: There is a pause, and Aldous looks at Mycroft, and Mycroft looks at the fire. In the end it is written down, in a long and cautious sentence that says nothing and could, in the proper hands, mean a great deal. You are aware that you have bought something. You are not yet sure what.

options.label: Refuse the Terms. Offer Advice, and Nothing More.
options.detail: You will not be a servant of the Crown, however benevolent. You will help, as a private gentleman, and no more.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You are proud, Sherlock. It is a quality I have always envied. I shall give you what I can, without terms, and I shall not pretend to be pleased.

options.outcome: Aldous coughs. The man from the Treasury looks at his initials. Mycroft, to everybody's surprise, smiles, slightly, and says that he had thought as much. He will give you what he can without any paper. It is less than you would have had, and it is clean.

options.label: Wait in the Corridor for an Hour.
options.detail: Your brother has not forgotten how things stood between you. It is a small, cold, Whitehall way of making the point.

quote.speaker: The hall porter
quote.text: Mr Mycroft will be a little while, sir. He has asked me to say that you are welcome to sit. He has also asked me to say that there is no hurry.

options.outcome: You sit on a hard chair in a long corridor and look at a portrait of a man who looks like a Lord Chancellor and, you suspect, was. The hour is exactly sixty minutes. When the door opens, Mycroft is behind it with his hands folded, and he says, with a face of perfect blandness, 'Ah. Sherlock. You are early.'

echoes.text: You know the price already. Mycroft named it in February, and has not once mentioned it since, which is how you know that he has not forgotten.

M2.title: Whitehall Wires
M2.description: Saturday, late afternoon. Whitehall in the dusk is a long, grey, hurrying street of lamps and clerks and shuttered windows, and behind every one of them a man is waiting to be told that something is not his department. Mycroft has given you a list of three doors. Behind the first is the Home Secretary's private secretary, who can sign a warrant that no magistrate may question. Behind the second is the Telegraph, which has the Professor's cables in a drawer. Behind the third is the Treasury, which can close an account with a single minute. You have time for one tonight.

options.label: Obtain the Home Secretary's Warrant.
options.detail: A single paper that opens every door in England. It is irregular, and effective, and will be remembered by those who dislike it.

quote.speaker: The Home Secretary's secretary
quote.text: The Secretary has signed it, Mr Holmes, with a good grace. I should add that he asked me to say that it is not a precedent. I am bound to say that it is a precedent.

options.outcome: The warrant is a single sheet of thick cream paper, with an embossed crest and a signature like a small black bird. You put it in your coat with the faint, unholy feeling of a man who has been handed a loaded gun in a church. It will open every door. It will also close several.

options.label: Read the Professor's Cables at the Telegraph Office.
options.detail: Every word he has sent in six months, in a drawer. It will take all night to read and cost your eyes.

quote.speaker: The chief of the Telegraph
quote.text: They are in cipher, sir. I should warn you that we have never broken it. But I have a young man who has been looking at it for a year, and he says it is not impossible.

success.outcome: By midnight you have the first key, and by four in the morning you have the second, and by dawn you can read a month of the Professor's private correspondence like a Sunday paper. It is cold, courteous, exact and nearly illegible with malice. You have never in your life been so tired, and so pleased.

failure.outcome: You work all night, and the cipher does not give. At six the young man falls asleep on the table, and you rise with a headache like a hammer and a long, slow, ugly sense of having wasted the Government's time. It is a small failure. It does not feel small.

options.label: Close the Professor's Accounts at the Treasury.
options.detail: A minute in the right hand, and his bank is told that it cannot pay. It is clean, bloodless and lawful, and it will not be forgotten.

quote.speaker: The man from the Treasury
quote.text: I shall have the instruction sent by messenger in the morning. The Bank of England will be most obliging. It is not often that it is asked to do something it actually wishes to do.

options.outcome: He writes four lines on a Treasury minute-sheet, folds it, seals it, and puts it in a leather case. The whole transaction takes ninety seconds and costs the Professor, you later estimate, a good deal over eleven thousand pounds. Nothing so elegant has happened to you since January, and you did none of it.

options.label: Let Lestrade Vouch for You.
options.detail: A word from a man the Yard respects. He can do it once. It will mend a good deal, and it will use up what he had.
options.outcome: Lestrade is gone an hour, and comes back with his collar undone and his hat in his hand. The Chief has agreed, he says, to take another look. The word goes round the building by noon. Doors that were closed are, for the moment, unlocked.

options.label: Walk the Whitehall Corridors as a Clerk.
options.detail: Nobody in a government building notices a clerk. You may go through any door that is not locked, and read any paper that is not under a cover.

quote.speaker: A messenger
quote.text: Mind the corner, sir. They'll have you for a Treasury man, and then you'll never get out. It's the third door on the left, and the second if you're quick.

options.outcome: You are three hours in the Home Office, and four in the Treasury, and nobody asks you a question except where the lavatory is. In the course of the afternoon you read the Professor's name on three minute-sheets, in three different hands, and a short, cold note to the Chief Clerk of the Bank in the sixth. It is not what you came for.

M3.title: The Second Ledger
M3.description:
Sunday 26 April. Mycroft takes you down a stone stair in the old part of the building, past three locked doors and a sleeping commissionaire, and into a small bare room with a deal table and a green-shaded lamp. On the table lies a book.

It is not the Professor's grey ledger. It is a smaller, older, tattier volume in black American cloth, taken in a raid on a Hatton Garden jeweller six years ago and never returned to the Yard. 'It was meant,' says Mycroft, 'to be burned.' He does not say who decided that it should not be.

options.label: Read It All.
options.detail: Every name, and every page. It will give you the Professor's whole hold on the powerful, and a good deal that a man might prefer not to know.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You will find six members of the Commons in it, Sherlock, and two of the Lords, and a bishop. I did not read it myself. I preferred to have it read to me, by a clerk, with the names left out. It was not the same.

options.outcome: It takes the night. You read the names, and the sums, and the notes in a spidery hand beside each: a debt, a woman, a signature, a Sunday afternoon. By morning you know a great deal about how England is governed, and a good deal more about what it costs. You come up into the grey light of Whitehall with the faint, sick feeling of a man who has read another man's letters.

options.label: Read the First Page and Close the Book.
options.detail: Enough to know what it is. The rest is a weight you need not carry.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You are wise, Sherlock. Or you are squeamish. In my experience they come to the same thing, and there is no shame in either.

options.outcome: One page is enough. It lists a dozen names, in a neat hand, and against each name a sum, and a date, and the single word 'held'. You shut the book. Mycroft nods, with the air of a man who has been spared something, and locks it in a drawer. You do not ask him what he intends. You have the sense that it will be better not to.

options.label: Refuse to Open It.
options.detail: You will not be party to what is in it. A detective's hands should not be in that book.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: As you wish. It will not make it any less true, you understand. It will only mean that I must go on carrying it by myself. I confess that I had hoped for a companion.

options.outcome: You push the book back across the table with one finger. Mycroft does not move for a long moment. Then he takes it, and puts it in his pocket, and says that you may find the way out yourself. You go up the stair alone, and you hear, behind you, the soft heavy sound of a man sitting down.

options.label: Take a Night at Watson's Fireside.
options.detail: Not a decision, a repair. You can do it once. You will come back to this scene a little less ragged, and a little behind.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are to sit in that chair, Holmes, and you are not to speak of the case. Mary has made a pie. I do not propose to argue.

options.outcome: You sleep in the armchair, in your boots, with a rug that smells of lavender over your knees. You wake at dawn with a stiff neck, a clear head, and the faint, foolish feeling of having been looked after.

echoes.text: The Home Secretary's warrant is folded in your waistcoat, a small cold square against your ribs.

M4.title: Special Branch
M4.description: Monday 27 April. Superintendent Greaves of Special Branch is a heavy, courteous, silent man with a grey moustache and the dull eye of one who has spent twenty years watching people who did not know they were watched. He sits in the corner of a bare room in Great Scotland Yard with a roll of paper on his knee, and he has thirty men. They are not policemen, quite; they do not wear uniforms, and they do not arrest anyone who is not on a list. He wishes to know, with great politeness, what you would like them to do. He would also like it understood that he does not ask why.

options.label: Strike the Professor's Own House With Special Branch.
options.detail: A quiet, silent, absolutely certain raid, with no newspaper and no inquest. They will take what is there and say nothing to anyone.

quote.speaker: Superintendent Greaves
quote.text: Thirty men, sir, and not one of them will say a word to the press. If there's a paper in the house, we'll have it. If there's a man in it, he'll go to a place that doesn't appear in the books.

success.outcome: The house is taken at three in the morning without a sound. The servants are collected, the doors are locked, and the study is sealed with wax. By dawn there is not a scrap of paper in it that has not gone to a vault in Whitehall. The Professor was not at home. But for the first time his house has been silenced, and the silence is a peculiarly ugly one.

failure.outcome: The house is empty, and has been for three days, and the papers with it. Greaves's men stand about in the dawn with a faintly embarrassed air. It is a perfect, silent, professional failure.

options.label: Hold Greaves's Men in Reserve.
options.detail: A man in reserve is a man who can be used when it matters. It is slower, and it is wiser.

quote.speaker: Superintendent Greaves
quote.text: In reserve, sir. Very good. I shall keep them where I can find them. A force is like a hat. It is best not to have it out until it is wanted.

options.outcome: Greaves nods, once, with the air of a man who has found a sensible customer. His thirty men go back to the work of looking at people who do not know it. You have lost a day, and kept a weapon.

options.label: Ask Greaves What He Really Thinks of the Professor.
options.detail: Twenty years of watching. A man in his position has seen the whole of the case, and has never been asked.

quote.speaker: Superintendent Greaves
quote.text: I think, Mr Holmes, that he's the only man in England who was ever quite sure of himself. It's what makes him dangerous. It's also what'll hang him, if anything does.

options.outcome: Greaves talks for an hour, flatly, in a voice like a man reading an inventory. He has been following the Professor's people for six years, and has never been allowed to touch them. He has a drawer of names and a drawer of dates and a short, dry, unforgiving verdict on every one. When he has finished he asks whether he has been of any use. He has been of the greatest.

echoes.text: Greaves has the Foreign Office clerk's file under his arm. He has the manner of a man who has seen a better coat than his own.
You have met the Superintendent before, at a Club that does not speak. He nods, once, as though it had been a funeral.

M5.title: A Minister's Visit
M5.description: Tuesday 28 April. He comes in a closed carriage, at nine in the evening, and refuses to give his name to Mrs Hudson, who nevertheless knows it. Lord Harcastle is an Under-Secretary of State, a tall, fair, handsome man of fifty with the weary courteous manner of a man who has never been refused anything, and he is plainly frightened. He sits on the edge of your sofa and turns his hat in his hands. He has heard, he says, that there is a book. He has heard that it contains a name. He has come, as a gentleman, to ask whether anything might be done.

options.label: Take What He Knows as a Source, and Spare Him.
options.detail: A frightened man who has seen the inside of the Professor's arrangements is worth a hundred ledgers. Let him buy his safety with what he can tell you.

quote.speaker: Lord Harcastle
quote.text: I will tell you everything I know, Mr Holmes. It is not a great deal, but it is more than I should care to see in the newspapers. I trust that I may rely on your discretion.

options.outcome: He talks for two hours, in a low voice, with his hat on his knee. He has dined with the Professor's friends, and lent them his name, and been lent a great deal of money in return. At the end he looks ten years older. You promise nothing. He seems to feel that you have. When he goes, you sit for a long time without moving, with an odd feeling about the way that things are done.

options.label: Refuse, and Warn Him to Resign.
options.detail: A man in his position can do nothing but go. It is better that he go on his own feet.

quote.speaker: Lord Harcastle
quote.text: You are hard, Mr Holmes. I had been told that you were a man of reason. I see that I was misinformed. You are a man of principle, and it is a much more uncomfortable thing.

options.outcome: He rises, and puts on his hat, and says that he will think about it. He resigns on Thursday, on the ground of ill-health, and goes to his estate in the north. The newspapers say that it is a pity. You do not. You find, to your surprise, that you do not feel better, only cleaner.

options.label: Hold It Over Him and Take What He Can Give.
options.detail: A man who owes you is a useful man. You will not use it often. You will know that you can.

quote.speaker: Lord Harcastle
quote.text: I perceive, Mr Holmes, that you have chosen your side. I should like to say that I admire it. But I think that you have chosen it very much as the Professor chose his.

options.outcome: He gives you his word, and his word is worth, you suspect, about what you offered for it. You note it in your pocket-book, with a date, in a small neat hand. It is not a pleasant thing to hold. You are aware, putting the book away, of a small cold sensation, as of a door that has not quite shut.

echoes.text: Greaves's men are in the street outside, in the shadow of the opposite house. Lord Harcastle did not see them. They saw him.
Greaves says, without being asked, that the Colonel has not been seen in London since Friday, and that it is the only thing that has worried him.

M6.title: The Bank's Quiet Room
M6.description: Wednesday 29 April. The Chief Cashier of the Bank of England receives you in a quiet, panelled room with a green carpet, a coal fire and a clock that ticks like a gentleman clearing his throat. He is a small, neat, grey man who has sat in the same chair for thirty years. He has received the Treasury's minute. He would like, he says, to ask what the Government wishes him to do about the Professor's money, which is large, intricate, and, in his considered opinion, not entirely creditable.

options.label: Freeze Every Account at Once.
options.detail: A sudden, total, silent stroke. The Professor's men will be paid nothing, and will notice it by Friday.

quote.speaker: The Chief Cashier
quote.text: Every account, sir? Very good. It will be done by noon. I should add that in thirty years I have never been asked to do so much harm with so little noise.

options.outcome: At noon the Professor's bankers are told, one by one, that their drafts will not be honoured, and by two o'clock the City has heard of it. By four there are seventeen men in London who have not been paid, and who do not know why. The Chief Cashier smiles, for the first time, a small, pleased, dry smile, as of a man who has hit the nail.

options.label: Let a Little Money Flow, and Follow It.
options.detail: A trickle can be traced where a flood cannot. Let him pay his people, and see who is paid.

quote.speaker: The Chief Cashier
quote.text: I can arrange a trickle, Mr Holmes. It will go to eleven accounts at six banks. I should be glad if you would keep a note of them, since I shall be asked to explain it one day.

options.outcome: For three days the Bank's clerks make notes of every payment, to every name, in every currency. By the end of the week you have a map of the Professor's people that no policeman could have drawn. It is a good map. But you have also, you are aware, allowed his men to eat for three days that they would otherwise have starved.

options.label: Leave the Money to the Courts.
options.detail: A freeze is an act of the Crown, and not a verdict. Let the law decide, in its own good time, who is entitled to what.

quote.speaker: The Chief Cashier
quote.text: A proper view, Mr Holmes. I shall do nothing at all. It is a thing I am good at, and I assure you that it is a much more difficult thing than it looks.

options.outcome: The Chief Cashier shakes your hand with a gentle, dry, delighted grip. The money stays where it is. In the weeks to come it is the subject of three lawsuits and an inquiry, and the Professor's men are paid in the interim.

options.label: Take a Night at Watson's Fireside.
options.detail: Not a decision, a repair. You can do it once. You will come back to this scene a little less ragged, and a little behind.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are to sit in that chair, Holmes, and you are not to speak of the case. Mary has made a pie. I do not propose to argue.

options.outcome: You sleep in the armchair, in your boots, with a rug that smells of lavender over your knees. You wake at dawn with a stiff neck, a clear head, and the faint, foolish feeling of having been looked after.

echoes.text: Mr Dunmore's name is on a slip in your pocket-book. The Chief Cashier does not know it, and you do not tell him, because you wish to see whether his face does.

M7.title: Terms From the Other Side
M7.description: Thursday 30 April. The solicitor comes to the Diogenes Club, which is itself a breach of every rule of the place, and is received by Mycroft in the Strangers' Room with a face as blank as a plate. He is a quiet, pleasant, elderly man named Thorne, who acts for a client who does not give his name. He has a document. It offers, in the most correct and dignified language, to surrender the original of the second ledger and every other paper in the Professor's possession, to leave England within the week, and never to return, in return for an assurance that no proceedings will be taken. Mycroft looks at you. He is, you realise, very much inclined to accept.

options.label: Back Your Brother: Accept the Immunity.
options.detail: The ledger is surrendered, the Professor leaves, and the names are safe. It is not justice. It is the best peace that the State can buy.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You are doing the right thing, Sherlock. I know that it does not feel so. It will not feel so for a good many years. But it is the right thing, and I am grateful.

options.outcome: Thorne reads the paper aloud, in a flat dry voice, and Mycroft signs it with a steady hand. The solicitor folds it, shakes hands all round, and goes away with the air of a man who has done an ordinary morning's business. It is quite quiet in the room for a long time after he has gone. Mycroft pours two glasses of sherry, and you drink yours, and neither of you says what you are thinking.

options.label: Refuse and Press On.
options.detail: The law cannot be bought, even by the Crown. A man who surrenders a ledger will have kept a copy.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You are making a great mistake, Sherlock. I do not say that you are wrong. I say that you are making a mistake. There is a difference, and the difference is about nine hundred men.

options.outcome: Thorne rises, folds his paper, and says that he regrets it. Mycroft says nothing at all. For the first time in thirty years you have defied him in front of a stranger, and the stranger has seen it. When the solicitor has gone, your brother turns his chair a quarter-turn to the fire. 'I am not angry,' he says. 'I am merely more tired than I have ever been.'

options.label: Make a Counter-Offer: the Ledger and the Professor.
options.detail: He surrenders the ledger and himself, to a court, in public. A grander and a riskier bargain, and one that he is likely to refuse.

quote.speaker: Mr Thorne
quote.text: I shall carry your reply to my client, Mr Holmes. I should tell you plainly that he does not like to be told what to do. But he has also been known to admire a clever answer.

success.outcome: The reply comes back by midnight, in a small, neat, cold hand: 'Agreed, on one condition. That Mr Sherlock Holmes shall conduct the prosecution himself.' It is the most arrogant paper you have ever read, and you are smiling. You accept it at once, before you can think.

failure.outcome: The reply comes back by midnight, and it is a single line: 'Declined, with regret.' It is signed with a cross. Mycroft reads it over your shoulder and says nothing. You have asked for the moon, and been refused, and your brother knows precisely what it has cost him to stand beside you while you did it.

options.label: Let Mycroft Find a Third Way.
options.detail: He has been looking at it all night. He knows a form of words that is neither the immunity nor the court.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: A closed arrest, Sherlock, and an open trial of the lesser men. It is not a pleasing arrangement. It is the only one that will do.

options.outcome: He lays it out in a quarter of an hour, in a voice like a man reading out a long and exact recipe. When he has finished you have no objection to make. It is the neatest piece of work you have ever seen him do, and you are not at all sure that you like what it means.
options.requiresHint: Needs your brother's full trust

echoes.text: On Tuesday a ship called the Teutonic will leave Southampton, with a gentleman aboard under another name. You know, because he told you himself, in a mild voice, in your brother's club.
Mycroft has been alone with the solicitor since the morning, and it shows: he is paler than usual, and a little more precise.

M8.title: The Cabinet Room
M8.description: Friday 1 May. The room is on the first floor of a building in Whitehall that does not appear in the guide-books, with a long green table, twelve chairs, and a portrait of the Queen. You sit at the end of it, with your hands on your knees. At the head of the table sits a man you have never met, whose face you have seen in a hundred cartoons, and who has been told, over breakfast, everything that you know. He asks, in a dry quiet voice, what you propose. Mycroft sits at his elbow, looking at the green cloth. Everything has led to this table, and to what you say at it.

options.label: Accept the Crown's Commission.
options.detail: A quiet post, a quiet salary, and every door in England. You will find the Professor's remnants for the Crown, and the Crown will see that nobody ever asks what you did.

quote.speaker: The Prime Minister
quote.text: We should be glad to have you, Mr Holmes. I will not say that we shall always agree. I will say that I have never yet been bored in the presence of a man who disagrees with me intelligently.

options.outcome: The commission is drawn up on the spot, by a clerk who has evidently done this before. It is a single sheet. It is entirely vague. It says that a Mr Sherlock Holmes of 221B Baker Street is to be given every assistance in the discharge of certain duties of a confidential nature. It is signed at the foot by three persons, of whom one is your brother. You do not look at him as you sign.

options.label: Take the Second Ledger to the Standard and Publish It.
options.detail: Every name, every sum, every date. The Government will fall. It will deserve to, and so will a good many other things.

quote.speaker: Mr Alderson of the Standard
quote.text: You are sure, Mr Holmes? I shall want the whole of it, and I shall print the whole of it. I should say, as a friend, that I have never seen a story that frightened me more.

options.requiresFlagHint: Needs to have read the second ledger

success.outcome: It runs on a Saturday, in eleven columns, without a word cut. By Monday three Members have resigned, a bishop has gone abroad, and the Home Secretary is closeted with the Prime Minister for six hours. By Wednesday the Professor's name is on every tongue in England, and on every lip in the House. It is the most extraordinary week of your life. Nobody can say afterwards that you did the easy thing.

failure.outcome: It runs on a Saturday, in six columns, with the worst of it cut by a nervous sub-editor and the rest denied, in a single sentence, by a Government spokesman. By Monday the story is a rumour, and by Wednesday a scandal about a newspaper. The names are never printed. The Professor, in his quiet room, reads the paper and does not so much as smile.

options.label: Take the Evidence to a Magistrate and Let the Law Run.
options.detail: In the open, with a warrant and a public charge, under the one condition that you made on the first day.

quote.speaker: The Prime Minister
quote.text: I did not think that you would hold to it, Mr Holmes. I confess that I am relieved. It is much easier to be governed by a man who has the courage of his clause.

options.outcome: The Prime Minister, after a long silence, nods once. Aldous makes a note. Mycroft says nothing, and the corner of his mouth moves, for a quarter of a second, in something that you would have taken for a smile on any other face. The warrant is issued before lunch. By evening the Professor is in a cell in Holloway, and the Cabinet Room has gone back to its ordinary business.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs the law's condition from the first day

options.label: Let the Professor Go Quietly, Under the Immunity.
options.detail: He surrenders the book and leaves the country. The names are safe. It is the arrangement that your brother wanted, and that you agreed to.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: Thank you, Sherlock. I shall not say what it has cost me. I shall say only that I have never in my life been so fond of you, or so frightened of what you might do.

options.outcome: The Professor sails from Southampton on the Tuesday, in a first-class cabin, under his own name, with two trunks and a violin-case. The Cabinet Room goes back to its business. In a locked drawer in Whitehall a small black book lies in the dark. You walk home along the Embankment, by yourself, in the soft grey light, with the gulls going over the river.

options.label: Walk Out of the Room.
options.detail: You will not serve, and you will not publish, and you will not plead. A man may refuse them all.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: Sherlock. Sit down. You are making an exhibition of yourself. Sherlock. Please.

options.outcome: You rise, bow to the Prime Minister, and go out of the room. In the corridor a footman holds your hat. Behind you, through the closed door, you hear a murmur of voices and the soft scrape of a chair. You go down the stair into the sunlight, and into Whitehall, and the Cabinet Room goes on without you.

options.label: Print the Second Ledger With the Editor's Backing.
options.detail: A friend at the Standard, an inspector who will stand behind you in the witness box, and a name or two you can prove. It is not a gamble. It is a campaign.

quote.speaker: Mr Alderson of the Standard
quote.text: I have Lestrade to swear to the chain of custody, Mr Holmes, and a Bishop's chaplain who will swear to the signature. I shall print it as a campaign. If they sue us, they shall have to explain the book.

options.outcome: It runs on a Saturday, in eleven columns, with every name sworn to, and nothing cut. Three Members resign by Monday. By Wednesday the Government has appointed a Commission, and by the end of the summer the Professor's name is the name of an inquiry. It is, everyone agrees, the most complete exposure of its kind in the history of the Press.
options.requiresHint: Needs the ledger read, the Yard's trust and a good name

options.label: Put His Own Cables on the Table.
options.detail: Four hundred and nine of them, in his own cipher, read by you, in the presence of the Prime Minister. There is no second ledger that can answer that.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: Where did you get these? They will do very well. They will do beautifully. I may say that I am prouder of you than I have the means to say.

options.outcome: You lay the sheets out on the green cloth, in order, and read the first aloud. By the third the Prime Minister has stopped looking at the portrait of the Queen. By the sixth he has asked for a pen. It is not a difficult argument. It is a perfectly simple one, in the Professor's own hand: his dates, his sums, his people, his lies. By evening there is a warrant, and a van, and a quiet corridor in Holloway.
options.requiresHint: Needs the cipher broken and the law written into the terms

options.label: Have Greaves Take Him at Southampton on the Tuesday.
options.detail: You know the day, the ship and the name. Special Branch has thirty quiet men. It is the neatest arrest that Whitehall could wish for.

quote.speaker: Superintendent Greaves
quote.text: Southampton, Tuesday, the Teutonic, under the name of Mr Alexander Bell? I shall have thirty men on the quay, sir, and twelve more in the second saloon. He will not be given the pleasure of being surprised. He will merely find that his friends have come to see him off.

options.requiresFlagHint: Needs the Professor's own word about his sailing

success.outcome: He walks up the gangway at ten in the morning in a grey travelling-coat, with a violin-case and a carpet-bag, looking at nothing in particular. At the top of it there are two quiet gentlemen, a warrant, and the hat of the Superintendent, which is raised. For one moment the Professor stops. Then, with extraordinary courtesy, he says that he is entirely at their disposal.

failure.outcome: He is not on the ship. He was never going to be. The name on the passenger list is a clerk's, and the violin-case belongs to a bewildered young man from Manchester. The Professor sailed on the Monday, from Cherbourg, in a small yellow steamer, with the Government's blessing. It was a good plan.

echoes.text: Lord Harcastle is not at the table. His chair has been moved a very little, and a clerk has been told not to look at it.
You never opened the book. It lies on the green cloth by Mycroft's elbow, black and unmarked, and you do not look at it.
In your breast-pocket is a key that fits four hundred and nine locks. It weighs nothing at all.
The Prime Minister has begun without you. You can tell from the way that the secretary looks at his watch, and then at you, and then away.
The room is yours for the hour before the Cabinet sits. Mycroft has had the chairs put straight, and the papers laid out, and he is sitting in the corner with his hands folded, looking pleased.
The cables in your pocket are a year old, and every one of them is true. You find that you hold them a little less firmly than you did.

10W.title: The Trunk in the Back Bedroom
10W.description: Friday 24 April, afternoon. The Professor is gone, and the sitting-room smells of his bay rum and your own pipe. In the back bedroom stands the old tin trunk in which you keep your faces: a priest's black, a sailor's jersey, a clerk's shiny coat, a box of paints, three false moustaches and a dead man's spectacles. If you are to be hunted, this is the hour for deciding whom you will be, and it is not a trifling question. A face is a thing that you put on in front of a great many people, and a good one is a thing that a man can live in for a week.

options.label: The Aged Italian Priest.
options.detail: Soutane, stoop, breviary. Nobody looks at a priest, and nobody asks him a question that he cannot answer with a blessing.
options.outcome: You take the black cloth from the trunk and put it on with the neatness of long practice. In the glass an old Italian gentleman looks back at you with a faint, benevolent anxiety. He has never in his life been accused of anything.

options.label: A Retired Master Mariner.
options.detail: A pea-jacket, a salt-stiff beard and a roll in the walk. He may sit in any public-house in London without being asked why.

quote.speaker: Your own reflection
quote.text: Forty years before the mast, and a bad leg from Valparaiso. Nobody argues with a bad leg.

options.outcome: The beard goes on with spirit gum, and the walk comes up out of your knees as if it had been waiting there for years. In the glass a weatherbeaten old man scowls at you, with a pipe between his teeth and an air of having seen a great deal that he does not propose to discuss.

options.label: A Clerk of the Better Sort.
options.detail: A shiny black coat, cuffs and a bowler. He is the most invisible man in the kingdom, and he may stand on any corner for an hour.
options.outcome: The coat is a little too tight across the shoulder, as a clerk's always is. You rub chalk into the cuffs, and flatten your hair with water, and in the glass a thin, pale, dispirited man in a bowler regards you with the faint reproach of one who has not been given his holiday.

options.label: Go as Yourself.
options.detail: No face but your own. If it comes to a fight they will know whom they are fighting, and so will you.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I think, Holmes, that you look best in your own face. I have always thought so. It is the only one that you cannot do badly.

options.outcome: You close the lid of the trunk on the priest, the sailor and the clerk, and lock it. It is not the most cunning decision of your career. It is, perhaps, the most honest, and the Professor, who has never in his life been honest, would be astonished.

K7.title: The Lady From the Opera
K7.description:
Tuesday 10 February. The note is on violet paper, scented with something expensive and faint, and it is signed with two initials and no address: I. N. It says that a lady whom you will remember would be glad of ten minutes of your attention at Briony Lodge, in St John's Wood, and that she will understand if you do not come.

You do remember. There was a King, and a photograph, and an evening in 1888 when you were beaten by a woman, and the memory has never stopped being instructive. She was Irene Adler. She is, by her note, Mrs Norton still, and she writes as one who is not accustomed to ask for things.

options.label: Call at Briony Lodge in Your Own Person.
options.detail: She will see through any other. You have never in your life been so sure of anything.

quote.speaker: Mrs Norton
quote.text: You have come as yourself, Mr Holmes. How civil. I had expected a clergyman with a bad leg.

options.outcome: She receives you in the same long, lamp-lit drawing-room, in a plain grey gown, with a book face down on the arm of her chair. She is a little thinner, and a little graver, and the voice is exactly as you remembered: a low, rich contralto with something dry and amused at the bottom of it.

options.label: Reply That the Professor Has You, and You Have No Time for Ladies.
options.detail: A courteous refusal. It is the sensible thing. You are not at all sure that you are being sensible.

quote.speaker: Mrs Norton
quote.text: I did not suppose that you would come. I had only thought that it would be as well to ask. There are not many people to whom I should write.

options.outcome: You send a line by return, on your own paper, in a steady hand. The reply is two words, in violet ink, and you do not show it to Watson. It says: 'Quite so.' You put it in the drawer where you keep the one photograph that you did not return. You are surprised to find that it is not a comfortable drawer.

K8.title: What Mrs Norton Knew
K8.description: Tuesday 10 February, in the drawing-room at Briony Lodge. She tells it plainly, as a woman tells a thing she has rehearsed and found shorter than she feared. In the winter a gentleman called, a Mr Hector Dunmore of the City, an agreeable man with a good tailor, and offered her a large sum for a certain photograph and a certain packet of letters that she has kept since 1888. He did not say who wanted them. He did not need to; the cheque he showed her was drawn on a bank in Lombard Street that you know. She has not sold. She has not burned them either. She would like, she says, to know what you would do.

options.label: Advise Her to Burn Them, and Ask Only for the Buyer's Name.
options.detail: A clean answer. She loses nothing, and you gain a name and a bank.

quote.speaker: Mrs Norton
quote.text: There. The name is Dunmore, and the bank is Brandt and Chambers. You will not tell me why you want it.

options.outcome: She lays the packet on the fire with a pair of tongs, and you watch the violet paper curl and go brown and then to nothing. Then she tells you everything she knows of Mr Dunmore, and it is a good deal. It is a name on a cheque, and a bank, and a habit of calling on Thursdays. 'You will tell me, one day,' she says, 'what you are about.' You say that you will, and are not certain it is true.

options.label: Ask Her to Sell Them, and Let You Follow the Money.
options.detail: She would be bait. It is a good plan. It is a poor thing to ask of her.

quote.speaker: Mrs Norton
quote.text: You wish me to be paid, Mr Holmes, and watched, and for the sake of a cheque I am not to see. I should like it noted that I do it with my eyes open.

options.outcome: She does it, and does it beautifully, and for a fortnight a small, shabby man follows a small, expensive cheque through four banks and a post office. At the end of it you hold the whole of a line of the Professor's money. She never refers to it again, and does not write. You tell yourself that she can look after herself. It is what she would say.

options.label: Tell Her to Leave London for a Season, and Keep the Packet With Her.
options.detail: A cold spring on the Continent, and a quiet name. You cannot protect her here. You may be able to see that she is not found.

quote.speaker: Mrs Norton
quote.text: I have been on the Continent before. You will be able to write to me through a bookseller in the Rue de la Madeleine, if you should ever have anything to say.

options.outcome: She is packed by Wednesday, with a smallness of luggage that you remember from before. At the door she turns, and puts out her hand, and you take it. 'I am glad,' she says, 'that it was you.' She does not say of what. By the time you have thought of an answer, the cab has turned the corner.

echoes.text: You have a cabman's name already. You do not offer it. She has a way of making people feel that they have said more than they have.

MX1.title: The Cable Room
MX1.description: Monday 27 April, six in the evening. The Telegraph Office's cable room is a long, brass-and-glass shed of clerks in sleeve-garters. The chief of the department, a dry little man named Fenn, has laid out on a table a year of the Professor's traffic: four hundred and nine cables, all in cipher, all sent to nineteen addresses, none of which has ever been opened. He has been looking at them for a twelvemonth. He is at once exhausted and pleased to be asked. He would like, he says, to be told what he is looking at.

options.label: Count the Groups in a Single Cable.
options.detail: Every cipher is made of something, and the first thing to learn is the size of its pieces.

quote.speaker: Mr Fenn
quote.text: Four figures to a group, Mr Holmes, and I have counted nine thousand of them. I have not thought to ask whether any of them was bigger than any other. It did not seem the sort of thing that mattered.

options.outcome: You go through three cables with a pencil, and the thing is plain in a quarter of an hour. Every group is four figures, and none is higher than four hundred. A cipher of that kind is not a machine. It is a book, a book of about four hundred pages, and the groups are the pages, and the lines, and the words.

options.label: Study the Hours at Which They Were Sent.
options.detail: A man's habits are a map of his mind. The Professor's must be extremely regular.

quote.speaker: Mr Fenn
quote.text: On the quarter-hour, sir, always. Fifteen minutes past, or the half, or a quarter to. I have a chart. It is a handsome chart.

options.outcome: The chart is handsome, and entirely uninformative. The Professor sends his cables at the quarter-hour because he is a man who does everything on the quarter-hour. It tells you a great deal about his character and nothing at all about his cipher. You are given a cup of tea.

options.label: Question the Clerk Who Sends Them.
options.detail: A nervous, plain young man who has been paid to forget. He may remember more than he has been paid for.

quote.speaker: The clerk
quote.text: He writes the first part out himself, sir, in a kind of violet ink, and he always writes it the same. I mean the beginning, that is. Five groups. It never varies. I used to think it was a sort of a signature.

options.outcome: The clerk is frightened, and then relieved, and at the end of a quarter of an hour tells you one small thing that nobody had asked him: that the beginning of every cable is the same. It is a small thing. You write it down, and underline it twice.

echoes.text: You carry into the cable room a clause that you would not give up, and Mr Fenn, who has not seen one before, looks at it with great respect.

MX2.title: The Opening Groups
MX2.description: Monday, seven in the evening. A clerk has brought a lamp, and a fresh pot of tea, and Mr Fenn has put on his spectacles with the air of a man about to be shown a conjuring trick. The cables lie in four stacks. Every one of them begins with the same five groups, as the clerk said, in the same violet ink. The rest is a flood of apparently random figures. If the opening is a signature, it should be a name. If it is anything else, it should be a clue. You have the time for one comparison before the room must be closed.

options.label: Take the Opening Five Groups as a Title, and Look for a Book.
options.detail: A man who begins every letter with the same five numbers is naming something, and in a book cipher what a man names is the book.

quote.speaker: Mr Fenn
quote.text: A title, sir? Then it is a title that has not got very many words. Five groups. Five words. I should say it was a book with a short name.

options.outcome: You count them out on your fingers, five words, and there is a book in your mind before you have finished. It is a short title, and an unusual one, and it belongs to the man who has written every one of these cables. 'The Dynamics of an Asteroid.' A treatise that not above a dozen men in Europe can read, and that no one would think to suspect of being a cipher key. You have never seen anything so arrogant.

options.label: Check the Last Groups: the Signatures.
options.detail: The end of a cable is as telling as its beginning. A man who always begins in the same way should always end in the same way.

quote.speaker: Mr Fenn
quote.text: They are not the same at all, sir. They are never the same at the end. I think he is only filling the line, to the length.

options.outcome: The ends are a jumble: nonsense, filler, a padding of numbers that run to the bottom of the form and stop. You spend a long half-hour on them and learn that the Professor is a tidy man who does not like a short line. It is not a thing you needed to be told.

options.label: Compare the Cables With the Weather Reports.
options.detail: A man who writes every day to nineteen addresses may be writing about something that happens every day.

quote.speaker: Mr Fenn
quote.text: I have a full set of weather reports, sir. I took the liberty. Nothing whatever. The weather in Brussels is what the weather is, and the Professor's figures have nothing to do with it.

options.outcome: The weather in Europe, over the past twelvemonth, is not a cipher. It is the weather. You close the folder with a firmness that makes Mr Fenn blink, and he thanks you, in a small voice, for having at least removed a hypothesis.

MX3.title: The Key
MX3.description:
Monday, nine in the evening. The cable room is empty but for you and Mr Fenn, who has taken off his sleeve-garters and is sitting upright on a stool, like a man at a revival. There is a pot of tea, a pile of paper, and a single cable laid out in the lamp-light.

Everything that the evening has shown you is on the table. It is for you to say, in words, what the Professor's cipher is, and how it may be read. Mr Fenn, who has spent a year on it, does not at all expect to be told.

options.label: Name the Key: His Own Treatise, by Page and Line.
options.detail: The groups are four figures, none above four hundred; the opening is a title. The Professor has written his cipher in his own book.

quote.speaker: Mr Fenn
quote.text: Page, line, word. Good Lord, sir. It is as simple as that. A year, and it is as simple as that. I shall want to sit down.

options.outcome: You have the first sentence in four minutes, with a copy of the treatise borrowed from the British Museum by a messenger who was very much astonished to be sent for it at ten at night. It is a cold, short, courteous message, the first of four hundred and nine, and it concerns the date and the hour of a bank transfer. By midnight you can read the whole of the Professor's correspondence for a year. Mr Fenn has not yet sat down.
options.requiresHint: Needs both traces: the size of the groups and the opening words

options.label: Venture That It Is a Book, and Leave It There.
options.detail: One trace, and a good guess. You will not be able to read the cables, but you will know why they cannot be read.

quote.speaker: Mr Fenn
quote.text: A book, sir? I had thought it was a code-word table. A book, though. Yes. I see that. I shall ask the Museum for every book published since 1860 with four hundred pages. It will take a year, I dare say.

options.outcome: Mr Fenn is grateful, and discouraged. It is a real piece of progress, and it is not enough. He promises to send a list of every four-hundred-page book in London to the Foreign Office, and you go home in a cab with the pleasant, thin sensation of a man who has been nearly right.
options.requiresHint: Needs one of the two traces

options.label: Hand the Cables Back Unread.
options.detail: You have not the key, and you will not pretend to have it. A tired man who guesses is a tired man who is wrong.

quote.speaker: Mr Fenn
quote.text: You are honest, Mr Holmes. It is a rare quality in this building. I shall go on looking at them, and I shall let you know if the Almighty is kind.

options.outcome: You thank him, and go home to sleep, with the faint, unpleasant sense of having let a good thing go by. Mr Fenn stays on in the cable room until three in the morning, looking at nineteen addresses and a violet signature, and goes home no wiser. In the morning the papers have nothing to say about it.

M6B.title: The Professor Calls on the Club
M6B.description:
Wednesday 29 April, nine in the evening. The porter of the Diogenes Club has never in forty years admitted a man to the Strangers' Room without a card, and he is, tonight, visibly unhappy. The card in his hand says 'Professor J.

Moriarty' in a good copperplate. Mycroft, to your astonishment, has said that he will see him. He sits at the head of the long table, vast and still, with his fingers laced, and says to you, quietly, that it is not a thing that he wishes you to see, and that it would be better if you did.

options.label: Receive Him in Silence and Let Him Speak.
options.detail: A man who has come to a club to be heard is a man who wishes to be listened to. Let him talk himself out.

quote.speaker: Professor Moriarty
quote.text: I am told that the Government wishes to be rid of me. I should like it understood that I am not at all difficult to be rid of. I sail from Southampton on Tuesday. I propose to leave quietly. I propose that nobody should see it.

options.outcome: He speaks for a quarter of an hour, in a mild voice, with his head swaying. He says nothing that he does not intend you to hear. Yet at the end of it you know three things that he did not mean to tell: the day, the ship, and the name that he will sail under. Mycroft's face does not alter. His fingers, on the table, have grown slightly white.

options.label: Test Him: Name the Arms of His Web That You Have Cut.
options.detail: A direct, bold, extremely rude thing to do in a club. He may flinch. He may not.

quote.speaker: Professor Moriarty
quote.text: You are very well informed, Mr Holmes. I shall have to speak to someone about it. In the meantime, I must tell you that you have counted one more than there are.

success.outcome: You name them one by one, the printer, the cab-yard, the bank, and at the fourth his head stops swaying. It is a small stop, as of a clock between two ticks. Mycroft sees it too. 'Quite so,' says the Professor, with a faint, good-humoured smile, and does not say another word on the subject. But he has lost a great deal of his composure, and you have not.

failure.outcome: He corrects you gently on three points, in a voice of great courtesy, and the third of them is correct. You find that you have named an arm of the web that does not exist, and he thanks you for the information. It is a long, silent, exceedingly uncomfortable ride home, in a cab that Mycroft has insisted on paying for.

options.label: Refuse to Sit in the Same Room.
options.detail: You will not be party to a bargain with that man. Your brother may do as he pleases.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You are making this very difficult, Sherlock. I do not say that you are wrong. I say that I shall now have to do it alone, and that I shall do it somewhat less well.

options.outcome: You rise, and bow to your brother, and go out into the hall, where the porter holds your hat with an expression of great sympathy. Through the closed door you hear nothing at all. It is the loudest nothing that you have ever listened to. When Mycroft comes out, an hour later, he looks ten years older, and says only that he has had a most interesting conversation.

B1.title: A Visitor in a Mask
B1.description: Tuesday 20 March 1888, a quarter to eight in the evening. A big man has come up the seventeen steps in a cloak of heavy fur and a boot-top of fur to match, and a black vizard mask covers his face from the cheekbones down. He announces himself as Count von Kramm. He is, quite clearly, nothing of the kind. He is the King of Bohemia, and he has a photograph to recover. Five years ago, in Warsaw, he was photographed beside a lady, and in a month he is to be betrothed to a princess of Scandinavia who would not like it. The lady's name is Irene Adler. She has said that she will send the picture to the family on the day the betrothal is made public.

options.label: Take the Case and Ask for the Whole of It.
options.detail: A client who hides half the story is a client who will be the death of the case. You will have all of it, or none.

quote.speaker: The King of Bohemia
quote.text: You are exact, Mr Holmes. Very well. There are letters as well. I wrote them to her. I was a young man, and I was not wise.

options.outcome: He tells it standing, with his back to the fire, walking up and down in large, heavy strides. It is a short story, and a stupid one, and entirely believable. You write down three dates and a street, and put the pencil away.

options.label: Tell Him You Know Who He Is.
options.detail: He has come in a mask to be a stranger. It costs you nothing to take it off him, and may put him in a more useful humour.

quote.speaker: The King of Bohemia
quote.text: You are right. I am the King. Why should I attempt to conceal it? I have come to you because I do not think another man in Europe can be trusted to be both discreet and clever.

options.outcome: You address him as Your Majesty, quietly, and explain that his Grand Duke's chin is on the coinage. He flings the mask on the table with a good deal of temper and a certain relief. It is, you think, a handsome, rather foolish face, and the first honest thing about him.

options.label: Ask for a Retainer and a Word That He Will Do as He Is Told.
options.detail: A king is no use to you in the way. If he wishes to be helped, he must be seen to be helped, and not to be helping.

quote.speaker: The King of Bohemia
quote.text: I am not accustomed to being given instructions. But I see that I have come to the right house. I shall do exactly as you say, and I shall hate it.

options.outcome: He gives his word with a bad grace, and a thousand pounds in notes, and an address in St John's Wood. It is the least pleasant interview of your week. It is also, as you may say to Watson in the morning, the only way to deal with a monarch.

B2.title: Briony Lodge
B2.description:
Wednesday 21 March 1888, three in the afternoon. Briony Lodge, in the Serpentine Avenue, is a small, tidy villa with a garden in front and a coach-house in the mews behind. The house is of the sort in which a retired person lives, who is not at all retired.

She is Mrs Godfrey Norton, as of this morning. She was married at St Monica's, in the Edgware Road, at the stroke of nine, to a young solicitor, and she went to the church in a landau, in a hurry, and was back by noon. You have three hours before the evening, and a street to learn.

options.label: Loaf About the Mews as an Out-of-Work Groom.
options.detail: A man in gaiters with a clay pipe, and plenty of time. The ostlers of St John's Wood will tell him anything.

quote.speaker: An ostler
quote.text: She's a quiet one, the Lady. Lovely to look at, and not a bit of fuss. There's a gentleman who comes by every day at three, a Mr Godfrey Norton, and he don't stop long.

options.outcome: You are a groom for two hours, and a bad one, but a likeable one, and the whole mews tells you its mind. In the course of the afternoon you learn what the lady eats, when she goes out, and which of the windows she sits in. And at the end of it you are called into the church, with an urgent shout, to be a witness, and are paid a sovereign for the pleasure.

options.label: Watch the Windows from Across the Road.
