options.detail: A man in a respectable coat on a bench, with a newspaper, is the least interesting thing in the street.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: Three visitors, one cab, a maid with a basket. At four she looks twice at the same carriage.

options.outcome: You see a good deal and understand a little. At four a gentleman with a handsome, dark, aquiline face calls, and is gone in twenty minutes, and the lady, who is a great deal quicker than she looks, sees you at the end of it. She does not say anything. She only looks, once, directly, as one looks at a clock.

options.label: Send Watson to Sit in the Lodge's Street.
options.detail: You will not need to watch yourself. You will need a man who can be relied upon to do exactly what he is told.
options.outcome: Watson is placed at the corner of the Serpentine Avenue, with a smoke-rocket under his coat, an instruction not to ask a question, and a face of such transparent honesty that the street takes him for a curate. He does it exactly as he is told. It is a quality that you have not, perhaps, praised enough.

echoes.text: The letters, the dates and the street are written on a single sheet in your pocket-book, in the order in which the King confessed them. It reads like the confession of a man who has lost something he is rather glad to have lost.
He has given you the name of his own country's chancellor, and the exact date of the betrothal. A man who is not afraid of being known is a man who is very much afraid.

B3.title: The Injured Clergyman
B3.description: Wednesday 21 March 1888, seven in the evening. The plan is a plain one, and it is not a pretty one. A man will be hurt in front of the lodge, and carried indoors by the kindly people of the house. And in the middle of the confusion a cry of fire will be raised. A woman, who has something to save, will go to the place where she keeps it. It will be the work of a minute. It is the oldest trick in the world, and it works, as the oldest tricks do, because it is cruel. You are lying in the road, in a broad-brimmed hat and a clerical coat, with a streak of red paint on your forehead.

options.label: Be Carried In, Hurt, and Watch Her Go to Her Hiding-Place.
options.detail: A good actor can be badly hurt for a quarter of an hour. A good watcher can see what she looks at.

quote.speaker: Mrs Norton
quote.text: Poor gentleman. Bring him in here, Jenkins. Put him on the sofa. And open the window, will you, it is a little close.

success.outcome: The cry of fire goes up, and the room fills with smoke, and Watson, outside, has done his work to the second. She does not scream. She goes at once, without a word, to the bell-pull by the fireplace, and half draws a panel behind it, and stops. It is an instant, and the whole case. You close your eyes and go on groaning, and you will remember the panel for the rest of your life.

failure.outcome: The cry of fire goes up, and she does not move. She stands in the middle of the room, in her plain grey dress, and looks across it at the injured clergyman, with an expression of the most polite attention. 'Mr Holmes,' she says, in a level voice, 'I am sorry that you have been hurt.' She does not ask how you came by the paint.

options.label: Refuse to Trick a Woman Who Has Done Nothing, and Search the House Another Way.
options.detail: She is a respectable wife, and you have no warrant. But there is the night, and a window, and you have plenty of practice.
options.outcome: You do not have the stomach for the fire-cry. You wait for the dark instead, and a window on the garden side, and the thirty seconds that it takes to find a strongbox, an empty one, and a bell-pull with a panel behind it. The panel is empty too. You leave a card on the mantelpiece, as you have never done before, and you are ashamed of it all the way home.

options.label: Wait Outside and Let Her Come Out.
options.detail: A woman who has something to hide moves it when she is frightened, and a woman who is frightened does not need your help.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: A cab at nine. A trunk at ten. Lamps out at eleven, and a note to the post.

options.outcome: You sit in the street, in the cold, with a pipe, and a patience that you did not know you had. At nine a hansom comes to the door; at ten a trunk goes up on the roof; at eleven the lamps go out one by one, and she is in the cab with a bag. It is a quiet departure, and a final one, and it tells you everything except the one thing that you need.

options.label: Go to Her Door in Your Own Name and Tell Her the Whole of It.
options.detail: You know what the King wrote, and what he wants, and you have stood in her mews in gaiters. There is only one honest thing left to try, and it is the one thing that Europe would never expect of you.

quote.speaker: Mrs Norton
quote.text: You have come to tell me the truth, Mr Holmes. I have been waiting four years for somebody to try it. Please sit down. I am not going to say anything for at least ten minutes.

options.outcome: She hears it all, in the lamp-lit drawing-room, without moving. When you have done she rings for tea, and says that she will not sell the photograph and will not use it, and will put it, with a letter of her own, in the safe of a firm in Lincoln's Inn, to be opened only if the King breaks his word to her. It is, she says, the nearest thing to a treaty that either of them has had. You carry the proposal to Baker Street in a cab, in the rain, a good deal lighter than you went.
options.requiresHint: Needs the King's whole story and an afternoon in her mews

echoes.text: A man in gaiters is married to a Mrs Norton, as a witness, in a church in the Edgware Road. You remember being paid a sovereign. You have never before accepted a tip.
Watson is at the corner of the Serpentine Avenue, with a roll of paper under his coat, holding a smoke-rocket as if it were a Bible.

B4.title: The Empty Alcove
B4.description: Thursday 22 March 1888, eight in the morning. Mrs Hudson says that there is a lady waiting in the street, and that the lady has gone. It is the old servant, she thinks. It is a pleasant, youthful voice, in a long coat, which wished you good morning, and walked quickly away. When you reach Briony Lodge the door stands open, the maid has been paid and sent home, and the drawing-room is empty. In the alcove behind the bell-pull is a letter, addressed to you, and a photograph of a woman in evening dress. The other photograph, the one that the King wants, is not there. It has gone with her, to the Continent, and she has left you her own portrait in its place.

options.label: Read the Letter and Take Her Portrait in Place of the Photograph.
options.detail: She has beaten you fairly. She asks for nothing, and she promises the King nothing. It is the clean thing to do.

quote.speaker: Irene Adler
quote.text: My dear Mr Sherlock Holmes: you really did it very well. I had not a suspicion until after the alarm of fire. I have been trained as an actress myself. I love and am loved by a better man than he. The King may do what he likes without molestation from one whom he has cruelly wronged.

options.outcome: You carry the letter and the portrait back to Baker Street, and you give the King the one and keep the other. He does not understand, and he is angry, and he offers you an emerald snake ring. You ask for the photograph instead, the evening-dress one, as a keepsake. It is your only fee. You will call her the Woman for the rest of your life.

options.label: Follow Her to the Continent and Take the Photograph.
options.detail: You have been beaten once. The King's money is good, and the boat is at nine. A clever man does not stop at the first defeat.

quote.speaker: Irene Adler
quote.text: I did not suppose, Mr Holmes, that you would be satisfied. I shall be at the Hôtel du Nord, and I shall be very much surprised if you do not come.

success.outcome: You are at Calais by evening and in Paris by morning, and in the dining-room of the Hôtel du Nord by the end of the week. She is alone, and reading, and does not look up. The photograph is in the lining of the book, and you have it out of her hand before she has finished the page. She smiles, a little sadly, and says that she is surprised it took you so long.

failure.outcome: She has gone before you reach Calais. There is a note at the first hotel, and another at the second, and a third in Vienna, in the same brisk hand, amused and a little weary. You are three weeks on the Continent. When you come home, tired and a little ashamed, the King is in the sitting-room, and he is not at all pleased.

options.label: Tell the King That It Is Safe, and Say No More.
options.detail: She has said she will not use it. A man who is told a half-truth by his detective is not the worse for it, so long as it lasts.

quote.speaker: The King of Bohemia
quote.text: You say that it is safe. You do not say that you have it. Mr Holmes, I am not a fool. I shall want that photograph, and I shall find someone else to get it.

options.outcome: He goes away unconvinced, with his mask in his hand. For a week the papers say nothing, and for a fortnight they say nothing, and in the third week they say a great deal. The betrothal is not announced. Somebody, somewhere, has begun to talk, and the King, who has been waiting, is no longer waiting for you.

echoes.text: You know exactly where the panel is, and you do not need to look. You also know that she knows you know.
You were found out at once, in the drawing-room, by a woman in a grey gown, and the memory has not stopped smarting.
There is a card on a mantelpiece in St John's Wood which says Sherlock Holmes, and you left it there like a fool.
You waited in the street all night, and she went anyway. It was a patient plan, and it deserved a better ending.
She looked at you once, from the window, as one looks at a clock. You think, now, that she looked twice.
The King's thousand pounds is in the drawer. You are not at all sure that you have earned it.

R1.title: Miss Stoner at Dawn
R1.description: Friday 6 April 1883, a quarter past seven in the morning. A lady in black, closely veiled, is shown into the sitting-room by a landlady who looks sleepy and anxious. She has come from Leatherhead by the dawn train, in a dog-cart, in the dark. She is shaking, and not from the cold. Her name is Helen Stoner. Two years ago her twin sister, Julia, died in the room next to her own, at midnight, in the dark, after unlocking her door and coming out into the passage. She said, as she died, a thing that nobody understood: 'Oh, my God, Helen, it was the band, the speckled band.' Last week Helen was moved into that same room. Last night she heard, from her bed, a low whistle.

options.label: Take the Case and Say You Will Come at Noon.
options.detail: She is in danger tonight, and it will not do to wait. But a quick look is better than a slow one, and a doctor in a hurry is a doctor who is easily seen.

quote.speaker: Miss Stoner
quote.text: Dr Roylott is going to London today on business. He will be away until the evening. I should be so glad if you could come while he is gone.

options.outcome: You say that you will be at Stoke Moran by one, and that she is to go home in the first train and say nothing. She goes without another word. You have been holding your pipe so tightly that the bowl has left a mark.

options.label: Ask What Her Stepfather Has, and What He Wants.
options.detail: A man who frightens a girl has a reason. Find the reason, and the means is generally at hand.

quote.speaker: Miss Stoner
quote.text: My mother's money comes to my sister and me when we marry, and not before, and the estate is nearly gone. He keeps a cheetah and a baboon in the grounds, and the gipsies are allowed to camp on the lawn. He had a practice in Calcutta, and a violent temper. He struck a native butler dead.

options.outcome: It takes ten minutes, and it is the most useful ten minutes of the morning. A mother's money, an income cut by a third at the day of each daughter's marriage, a man who has not got long to wait. You have not yet seen the room, but you already know why the room is dangerous.

options.label: Send for the Police Surgeon Before Going Further.
options.detail: A second opinion on a dead girl would be useful. A second opinion on a living one, who may be dying, is more useful still.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I have looked at her, Holmes, and she is not ill. She is afraid, which is a great deal harder to treat, and a great deal more serious.

options.outcome: Watson sees her at the breakfast-table, and writes a prescription that he does not intend her to take. It is mostly a pretext to keep her in the house until the train. He says, at the door, that he has never seen a healthier woman look so near to death.

R2.title: Stoke Moran
R2.description:
Friday 6 April 1883, a little after one in the afternoon. Stoke Moran is an old Surrey manor, with a gabled centre and two curving wings, of which one is in ruins. Dr Grimesby Roylott is away in London; Helen is waiting on the lawn.

She shows you the three bedrooms in a row. The room that was her sister's, and is now hers, has a bed clamped to the floor, a bell-rope that does not ring, and a ventilator that opens into the next room, and not the open air. You have two hours, a lens, a tape-measure, and a growing certainty that you do not like it here.

options.label: Examine the Bed, the Bell-Rope and the Ventilator.
options.detail: A bed that cannot move, a rope that rings nothing, a hole between two rooms: it is a puzzle that anyone would see at once, and no one would think to ask.

quote.speaker: Miss Stoner
quote.text: The ventilator was made two years ago, at my stepfather's order, and the bell-rope at the same time. I had thought it was a workman's foolishness.

options.outcome: The bell-rope is a dummy: it is tied to a hook above the ventilator, and goes nowhere. The ventilator is a hole between two rooms with a little brass grille. The bed is bolted to the floor so that the sleeper must lie exactly under both. You say nothing at all for some time, and then, quietly, you ask for a saucer of milk to be sent in.

options.label: Look Through the Doctor's Room: the Safe and the Saucer of Milk.
options.detail: A man's room is a man's mind. It may be dangerous to look at it unaccompanied, but it is quicker than waiting for him to speak.

quote.speaker: Your own reflection
quote.text: A safe, a chair, a small table, and a bit of string with a loop at the end. I do not at all like it.

success.outcome: In the quarter of an hour that you have the room to yourself you see a saucer of milk on top of the safe, a dog-lash with a loop in it. A drawer which smells faintly of something that is neither a dog nor a cat. You do not touch anything. You do not need to. By the time you have gone out by the window you have the whole thing in your mind in order.

failure.outcome: A step in the passage, and a voice, and the great shoulders of Dr Grimesby Roylott fill the doorway, a full two hours before his time. He says nothing at all. He takes up the poker from the grate, and bends it in his hands into a curve, and throws it into the fire. 'I am the Dr Roylott of Stoke Moran,' he says, 'and you will take yourself out of my house.'

options.label: Question the Housekeeper and Walk the Grounds.
options.detail: A cheetah, a baboon and a camp of gipsies are not the same as a plot. But they are all a part of how the house is kept.

quote.speaker: The housekeeper
quote.text: He has a lot of animals from India, sir, and he lets them out in the evenings. He says that it keeps the thieves away. I do not know. I would not go out in the park after dark, not for a pound.

options.outcome: The cheetah follows you with its eyes. The baboon is asleep. The gipsy women at the edge of the wood have nothing to say to you whatever. It takes an hour, and it gives you a feeling for the place that you do not at all want. It also gives you the one thing that you need: that nobody in the house has ever been into the room at night.

echoes.text: You know what the money is, and when it is to be paid. The Doctor has three months and a marriage to prevent.
You told Miss Stoner that you would come at noon. It is now past one, and you are conscious of being late.

R3.title: The Dark Room
R3.description: Friday 6 April 1883, eleven at night. The Doctor has come home, and eaten, and shut himself up in his room with the door locked. A single light shines from his window. You and Watson sit in the dark in the sitting-room of the Crown Inn, across the lawn, until it goes out. Then you cross the park together, through the shrubs, and in by the window of the room that is to be Helen's. She has gone to her aunt's, at Harrow, for the night. The ventilator is there, and the bell-rope, and the bed. You have a plan. It is a short one, and it begins with a lantern turned low.

options.label: Wait in Helen's Room with a Cane, in the Dark.
options.detail: A cane, a match and a steady hand. If the thing comes down the rope, it will come in the dark, and it will come to the bed.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are to sit in the dark in a murdered girl's bed, Holmes, with a cane, waiting for a snake. I should like it understood that I do not at all think much of the idea.

options.outcome: You sit through the hours with your chin on your hands, and the lantern shuttered, and the only sound in the world is the wind in the eaves. At half past twelve a light flashes in the Doctor's window and goes out. It is the longest silence that you can remember.

options.label: Put Watson at the Window with a Revolver.
options.detail: A second pair of eyes, and a second pair of hands. The thing might come in either way, and a doctor has the steadier nerve.
options.outcome: Watson takes up his post beside the open shutter, with his old Webley across his knee, and you hear him settle himself as he used to in the Maiwand ditches. It is a comfort that you do not say aloud. At the other side of the room you sit on the bed with your cane across your lap.

options.label: Confront Dr Roylott at His Door and Warn Him Off.
options.detail: A man who is told that he is known will, in general, think better of what he has not yet done. It is a bold stroke, and a dangerous one.

quote.speaker: Dr Roylott
quote.text: You are Holmes, the meddler. Take care that you do not meddle with me. I have broken better men than you across my knee.

options.outcome: He is in the doorway before you have finished your sentence, a huge, red, furious figure, in a dressing-gown. He says nothing that a jury would hang him for. But he looks at your throat, and then at Watson's, and goes in again, and locks the door. For a long quarter of an hour you cannot hear anything at all. It is, perhaps, an advantage. It is certainly a warning.

echoes.text: The bell-rope is a dummy, tied to a hook above the ventilator. You look at it once, with your lantern, and then do not look at it again.
A saucer of milk is on the safe in the next room. You do not at all like the thought of what it is for.
From the lawn comes the faint grunt of the baboon. It is not the thing you are afraid of, but it does not help.
A poker lies bent in a fireplace in the next room, as if it were made of wax. You do not intend to be in the next room.

R4.title: The Whistle
R4.description: Saturday 7 April 1883, three o'clock in the morning. It comes at last: a low, gentle whistle from the next room, and then a rustle, a faint metallic clang, as of the grille being slipped aside, and the very slight, patient sound of something coming down a rope. You strike a match. In the sudden yellow light a thing hangs from the bell-pull: a banded, yellow-brown, diamond-patterned head and a thick, puffed neck, swaying a little, as it feels for the bed. You have, perhaps, three seconds.

options.label: Strike at the Rope with the Cane and Drive It Back.
options.detail: A swift, hard blow, and then a noise to turn it. If it goes back the way it came, it will find the man who sent it.

success.outcome: The cane comes down across the rope with a crack, and the thing is gone in a flash of yellow, with a hiss like a boiling kettle. A moment later, from the next room, there is a terrible cry, and a sound of something heavy falling. When you light the lantern, the Doctor is sitting upright in his chair, with his head thrown back, and round his brow is a peculiar yellow band, with brownish speckles.

failure.outcome: The cane meets the rope a half-second too late. The thing is on the bed, and the bed is not empty: you have forgotten that in the dark the two shapes are the same. A cry, and a heavy fall, and a long silence. When the lantern lights it is Watson, grey and sweating, who is kneeling by the bedside, and he looks up at you and says nothing at all.

options.label: Light the Candle and Go for the Door.
options.detail: A shot at the thing would be as likely to hit the girl's room as the snake. A man in a locked house must let the house be opened.

quote.speaker: Dr Roylott
quote.text: Holmes. The door is locked. You are in my house, in the night, and I am going to be extremely angry in a very few moments.

success.outcome: You are in the passage before the thing has found the bed, and you put your shoulder to the Doctor's door and it gives. He is on his feet with a face of such fury that you step back. Behind him, on the safe, the saucer is empty. In the half-light the thing is coiled upon the chair; it lifts its head; and the Doctor, who has been tired for a long time, is bitten once, at the throat, before either of you has moved.

failure.outcome: The door is locked, and the passage is dark, and by the time you have the door down the thing has gone back by its own road. The Doctor is in his chair with a face like marble and a hand on the poker, and no sign of anything in the room except a small, closed basket on the safe. He will say that you broke in. He will say it extremely well, and a Surrey magistrate will believe him.

options.label: Pull Miss Stoner Clear and Wait for the Constables in the Morning.
options.detail: She is not there. But you can leave the room, and the house, and let the law take a sleeping man in his bed. It is the safe way, and the dull one.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: We shall be the laughing-stock of Surrey, Holmes, if we take a man in his nightcap for owning a snake. But I think that we shall be alive.

options.outcome: You go out by the window, quietly, as you came, and Watson follows. At dawn the constables arrive, a sergeant and two men, and find the Doctor in his chair, asleep, with a hot cup of tea. There is no snake. There is a basket, and a milk-saucer, and a civil gentleman who will say that he never saw you in his life.

options.label: Take the Snake Alive: Hold a Sack Over the Ventilator.
options.detail: You know the motive and you know the method. A man who sends a creature down a rope can be shown the creature, and a coroner cannot call a snake in a sack a misadventure.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You mean to catch it, Holmes. Alive. In a pillow-case. I have been in a good many tight places with you, and I do not think that any of them has been so small.

options.requiresHint: Needs the motive learned at dawn and the dummy rope found

success.outcome: The sack goes over the grille at the first whistle, with a sail-maker's knot at the neck and Watson's hands on the cord. The thing comes down the rope into the dark, finds the bag instead of the bed, and is a heavy, angry, lashing weight at the end of your arm. You carry it out through the window into the park, and you do not at all enjoy the walk.

failure.outcome: The knot is the wrong knot. The sack gapes, and the thing is out of it and into the dark of the room with a hiss like a kettle, and by the time the lantern is lit it has gone back by its own road. There is a sound of someone falling in the next room. When you reach him, he is beyond all help, and there is nothing left for you to prove.

echoes.text: You have been sitting up since midnight, in a murdered girl's bed, with a cane, and you are sure that nothing in the world is more peaceful than a snake.
Watson is at the window with his revolver. You are glad of it, and you do not say so.
Dr Roylott knows that you are here. He is not at all asleep, and he is not at all afraid.
The police surgeon has seen her, and signed a paper. If it is a murder, it will be a murder on the record.

G1.title: The Goose and the Hat
G1.description:
Friday 27 December 1889, the second morning after Christmas. You are on the sofa in your purple dressing-gown, with a pipe-rack at your head, and an old and seedy felt hat beside you. It was left by a gentleman who had been in a fight in Tottenham Court Road at four on Christmas morning, with a goose.

The gentleman fled. The goose was taken in charge by Peterson, the commissionaire, who is at this moment standing in the doorway, white as paper, with a thing in his open hand. It is the size of a small bean, and it blazes like an electric point. It was in the crop of the goose.

options.label: Read the Hat.
options.detail: A hat is a surprisingly intimate piece of clothing. It will tell you a great deal about the man who wore it.
options.outcome: You hold it up to the window and turn it in the lens. He is a man of intellect, who has lately fallen on evil days. Of a retiring habit, with little thought for himself. Whose wife has ceased to love him. Who has gas laid on in his house; and who does not wash his hair. You say it all in one breath. Watson stares at you, and then at the hat, and then at the carpet.

options.label: Put an Advertisement in the Evening Papers.
options.detail: The gentleman will want his hat and his goose. He will see it, and he will come.

quote.speaker: Peterson
quote.text: I have taken it to the Standard, sir, and the Globe, and the Pall Mall, and the Echo. They'll all have it by six.

options.outcome: You write a plain notice: that a goose and a black felt hat have been found, and may be claimed by Mr Henry Baker, whose initials are in the lining, at half past six, at 221B. You have not the least doubt that the name is a true one. Peterson puts the notice into four envelopes, and runs.

options.label: Test the Stone with a Glass-Cutter.
options.detail: It might be paste, and it might be the Countess of Morcar's missing blue carbuncle. A diamond scratches glass. Paste does not.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are scratching the window-pane, Holmes. It is the Countess of Morcar's carbuncle, and you are scratching Mrs Hudson's window with it.

options.outcome: It cuts a clean white line through the glass without effort. You lay it down on the table and look at it for a long minute. It is a large, pure, blue stone, and you can see in it, plainly, the entire history of a crime that is not yet a crime. 'It is a nice little case,' you say. 'There are four people in it, and none of them is a villain.'

G2.title: Mr Henry Baker Calls
G2.description: Friday 27 December 1889, half past six in the evening. Henry Baker is a large man with rounded shoulders, a massive head and a broad intelligent face tapering down to a pointed beard of grizzled brown. He has a touch of red in nose and cheeks, and a slight tremor of his extended hand. He wants his hat. He does not at all want his goose, which has been, regrettably, eaten; but you have bought him another, from the same market, and it hangs on the hook. Once he has taken it, he will leave, and there will be no cause to see him again. There is a thing that you need first.

options.label: Give Him a Fresh Goose and Learn Where His Own Came From.
options.detail: He bought it at the Alpha Inn, on a goose-club. The landlord of the Alpha got his geese from a salesman in Covent Garden. It is a chain, and you are at the end of it.

quote.speaker: Henry Baker
quote.text: I bought mine of the landlord of the Alpha, sir, in Museum Street. He has a goose-club, and we pay a few pence a week, and at Christmas we each have a bird. It was an excellent one. I would not have lost it for the world.

options.outcome: He takes the fresh goose with the stiff gratitude of a man who has lost a hat and a dinner. He is entirely innocent. He knows nothing of a stone; he has never been in Brixton; he has only a fixed idea that a hat should be returned. You do not tell him what was in the crop. He is a man who would take it hard.

options.label: Tell Him the Truth and Ask Him to Sit.
options.detail: He is an honest man, and has a right to know. A man who is told the truth will, as often as not, repay you for it.

quote.speaker: Henry Baker
quote.text: A jewel, Mr Holmes? In my goose? I think I shall have to sit down. And I think that I shall have to say that the Alpha Inn has very much more to answer for than I supposed.

options.outcome: He takes it quietly, and he takes it well. He says that he has been a poor man for a good many years and has learned not to be astonished. Then he tells you, at some length and with surprising shrewdness, the name of every man in the goose-club. He is a good witness. He would have been a better detective than most you have met.

options.label: Say Nothing of the Stone and Send Him Home.
options.detail: The fewer people who know what was in the goose, the fewer people there are to come looking for it.

quote.speaker: Henry Baker
quote.text: A good evening to you, sir. I am much obliged. I shall always say that Mr Holmes was a gentleman.

options.outcome: He goes down the seventeen steps with his goose under his arm and his hat on his head, and the stairs creak after him in their long, familiar way. It is a small deception, and a kind one. You find, after he has gone, that you are pleased with yourself, and not at all sure that you ought to be.

G3.title: Covent Garden by Gaslight
G3.description: Friday 27 December 1889, nine at night. The market is shutting, and the great flaring gas-jets are being turned down one by one. At the stall of Mr Breckinridge, in the poultry row, the salesman is counting out the last of his barrow, a stout man with a pair of sporting whiskers, and on the other side of the stall, in the shadow, a small, ferrety, frightened man in a long coat is asking the same question that you have come to ask. You have heard the question put twice. It is not a thing that a man asks idly. It is: where did the Brixton geese go?

options.label: Bet the Salesman That He Is Wrong About His Geese.
options.detail: A man will tell you anything to win a bet, and especially the price that he paid.

quote.speaker: Mr Breckinridge
quote.text: Wrong about my geese? Bred in the country, every one of them! I'll lay you a sovereign they came from Norfolk. I'll lay you five, you being so uncommonly civil about it.

success.outcome: He is on the bet before you have finished speaking, and the book comes out of his pocket. The sale of the geese is read out aloud for the crowd: forty to the Alpha Inn and a dozen to the Cosmopolitan. They were had from a Mrs Oakshott of Brixton Road. You pay your sovereign with real pleasure.

failure.outcome: He is extremely sharp, and he sees through it at once. 'You have come for the same as that other gentleman,' he says, 'and I will tell you what I told him. What I have sold is no concern of yours.' A pair of burly porters appear at your elbow. You leave more quickly than you came.

options.label: Ask Plainly and Pay for the Answer.
options.detail: A direct question and a sovereign. It is the simplest way and the dearest.

quote.speaker: Mr Breckinridge
quote.text: A sovereign for the name? I do not sell names, sir. But I do not mind saying that it is Mrs Oakshott, of 117 Brixton Road, and that you might ask her yourself.

options.outcome: He pockets the coin without looking at it, and gives you the name and the road. It is the quickest ten minutes of your evening, and it costs you something. When you turn round, the little ferrety man has gone from the shadow, and you have the unpleasant sense of having been heard.

options.label: Follow the Ferret-Faced Man.
options.detail: He asked the question for the same reason that you did. Whatever he knows about the geese, he is more frightened by it than you.

quote.speaker: The little man
quote.text: Don't. Don't, please. I have done nothing. I only want to know where the goose went. I am not a bad man, sir, I swear it.

options.outcome: You follow him through three streets and a passage, and take him by the arm at the corner of Henrietta Street. He is the thinnest, whitest, most frightened man that you have ever held. He gives his name as James Ryder, and says he is head attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan, and that he has not slept for two nights. You take him back to Baker Street in a cab.

echoes.text: The Alpha Inn is behind you, with its goose-club and its hat and its landlord, and you are now at the other end of the chain.
Henry Baker knows what was in his goose, and has promised to say nothing. You believe him.

G4.title: Mr James Ryder
G4.description:
Friday 27 December 1889, eleven at night. James Ryder sits in the basket-chair by the fire, with his hat on his knee, and he cannot stop shaking. You have told him, quietly, what you know: the Countess of Morcar's room at the Cosmopolitan, the plumber John Horner who was blamed, and the jewel-case which you suspect that he emptied.

You have laid the blue stone on the table between you. There is no more to be said, except what is to be done with a man who stole it and let another be taken. You have, in your own pocket, the means to ruin him; and on the mantelpiece, an unopened letter from the Yard.

options.label: Let Him Go. It Is Christmas.
options.detail: He is a weak man, not a wicked one. He has been frightened half out of his wits, and Horner can be cleared by a word. It is not a bad day for mercy.

quote.speaker: James Ryder
quote.text: God bless you, sir! God bless you! I'll leave the country, I'll go to Canada, you will never hear my name again. I swear it on my mother's life.

options.outcome: You open the door yourself, and say that he may go. He goes, down the stairs, in a sort of stumbling run, and you hear the street door bang. 'After all, Watson,' you say, 'I am not retained to supply the deficiencies of the police. If Horner were in danger it would be another thing; but this fellow will not appear against him, and the case must collapse. I suppose that I am commuting a felony. But it is the season of forgiveness.'

options.label: Send for Lestrade and Give the Stone to the Police.
options.detail: He has stolen a jewel and let an innocent man go to gaol. It is not your place to forgive him; it is the law's.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: The Countess's carbuncle, Mr Holmes, and the man who took it. That's two clever things in a night. I'd say it was a good Christmas.

options.outcome: Lestrade arrives within the hour, with a constable and a cab. Ryder goes without a word, grey and quiet, and does not look back. The stone goes to the Countess by messenger in the morning, and the plumber Horner is released by noon. It is, by every standard, a correct result. Watson says so, twice. You say nothing at all.

options.label: Take His Confession in Writing and Keep It Over Him.
options.detail: A confession in your pocket is a guarantee of his conduct for the rest of his life. It is a useful instrument, and a cold one.

quote.speaker: James Ryder
quote.text: You will have it in writing, Mr Holmes? Then I will write it. I will write anything. Only do not send me to prison.

success.outcome: He writes it in a small, wavering hand on four sheets of your own paper, and signs it, and weeps. You blot it, fold it, and put it in the drawer where you keep the things you do not intend to use. He goes out into the Christmas night a free man, and will keep, you think, remarkably straight.

failure.outcome: You have the pen in his hand, and the paper on the table, when he rises, white as the page, and goes through the door and down the stairs in one bound. By the time you reach the street he is a hundred yards off, running, and you hear a cab. The stone is on the table. The man is gone. And in the morning there is a letter from Lestrade, and it is not a pleasant one.

options.label: Ask Them All to Baker Street for New Year's Eve.
options.detail: Henry Baker, who knows the truth, and Mrs Oakshott, who reared the geese, and Peterson, and John Horner, who has been in a cell. And James Ryder, to be sat in the middle. It is a dinner, and it is a trial, and it is the only one in London that could end in a toast.

quote.speaker: Henry Baker
quote.text: You mean me to sit at my own table with the man who put a stone in my goose. Mr Holmes, I have been a poor man for a good many years, and I find that I have a great deal of spare charity. I shall be very much surprised if I do not need it all.

options.outcome: It is the strangest dinner that Mrs Hudson has ever laid. Ryder sits between the hat and the plumber and eats nothing, and is looked at with more than a little mild curiosity by a stout widow from the Brixton Road, and at the end of the second course he stands up, white as the cloth, and tells it all. Nobody says a word. Then Henry Baker, who has not at any point raised his voice, passes him the sprouts.
options.requiresHint: Needs Henry Baker told the truth, and Mrs Oakshott found

echoes.text: Mrs Oakshott of Brixton Road reared the geese, and sold them to a man who sold them to a man. It was she who gave you the whole of the chain.
You were turned away from the stall once, and you do not like being turned away.
A sovereign went into Mr Breckinridge's pocket for a name. You are not at all sure it was well spent.
You took a frightened man by the arm in Henrietta Street. You can still feel the thinness of it.
You read a hat, and were right about the gas.
Four evening papers carry your notice of a goose and a hat. You are proud of the prose.
There is a white scratch in Mrs Hudson's window that she has not yet spotted.
Henry Baker thinks he ate his goose in peace. You have not corrected him.

L1.title: A Red-Headed Pawnbroker
L1.description: Saturday 11 October 1890, ten in the morning. A stout, florid gentleman with a red head has come up the seventeen steps and is sitting on the edge of the basket-chair with his hat on his knee. His name is Jabez Wilson, and he keeps a small pawnbroker's business in Saxe-Coburg Square, in the City, with an assistant who will work for half wages. Eight weeks ago his assistant showed him an advertisement. It offered four pounds a week to any red-headed man of full age who would sit for four hours a day in an office in Pope's Court and copy out the Encyclopaedia Britannica, and Mr Wilson got the place. This morning he went to the office, and found a card on the door that said that the Red-Headed League was dissolved. He is not at all upset about the money. He would like to know what it was for.

options.label: Take the Case and Ask for the Whole of It.
options.detail: A man who has been paid four pounds a week to copy the Encyclopaedia has been paid to be out of his shop. It is the shop that is interesting.

quote.speaker: Jabez Wilson
quote.text: It was always from ten to two, Mr Holmes, and I never saw any League but a Mr Duncan Ross, who was polite and wore a bowler hat. He used to look in at the end of the day and pay me in sovereigns. I did think it was queer, but I thought that it was queer in my favour.

options.outcome: He tells it with more than a little detail and an immense relish, from the day the assistant, Vincent Spaulding, came to the shop, to the morning of the card on the door. You ask four questions. At the end of the fourth you have a pipe lit, and your eyes shut, and Watson, on the sofa, is looking at you with the face of a man who has seen it before. 'It is quite a three-pipe problem,' you say, 'and I beg that you won't speak to me for fifty minutes.'

options.label: Ask About the Assistant Who Works for Half Wages.
options.detail: A man who works for half pay is either a saint or has something to do in the shop that the pay would not allow.

quote.speaker: Jabez Wilson
quote.text: Spaulding? A smart fellow, Mr Holmes, though I don't know that I should have kept him at half wages if he hadn't been so good at the photography. He is always down in the cellar, developing his plates. It is his one fault. He takes an hour at it.

options.outcome: You ask him to describe the man, and he does so at some length. The assistant is short, and quick, and clean-shaven, with a white splash of acid upon his forehead, and ears that have been pierced for earrings. He is a clever man who is willing to work for half pay, and who spends an hour at a time in your client's cellar. You give no sign of what you think. You merely observe, in the course of the next moment, that there is no better evidence in the world than a man's own cellar.

options.label: Look at the Card on the Door of the Office.
options.detail: A card is a document. It will tell you at least as much as a story, and it cannot embroider.

quote.speaker: Jabez Wilson
quote.text: I have it in my pocket, Mr Holmes. I took it off the door. It says that the League is dissolved, and the date is the ninth of October, 1890. I thought it a civil way to end a matter.

options.outcome: He gives it to you, with some pride. It is a square card, in a good, plain hand, on a better paper than the occasion deserved. It is dated two days ago, and signed with a name that does not appear in any directory in London. You turn it over, and look at the back of it, and then, without a word, hold it to the light of the window. 'It has been written,' you say, 'by a man who was in a hurry, and who did not expect to be read.'

L2.title: Saxe-Coburg Square
L2.description: Saturday 11 October 1890, early afternoon. Saxe-Coburg Square is a shabby, genteel place, a square of dingy two-storeyed houses of brick looking out upon a small railed enclosure where a lawn of weedy grass and a few clumps of faded laurel-bushes make a hard fight against a smoke-laden and uncongenial atmosphere. On the corner house, three gilt balls and a brown board with Jabez Wilson in white letters announce the premises of your client. On the far side of the corner, a dull, shabby street runs back to a bright, busy one. It is the back of a bank.

options.label: Thump the Pavement and Knock at the Door.
options.detail: You will not go in. You will merely strike the stones with your stick, outside the shop, and see which of them are not stones. And then ring the bell, and look at the man who opens it.

quote.speaker: Vincent Spaulding
quote.text: Yes, sir? Was it Mr Wilson that you wanted? He is out, sir, but I am sure that I could oblige. I am the assistant.

options.outcome: The pavement is sound. The man at the door is not what you expected: he is quick, clean-shaven, clever, and has about him the look of one who has spent a great deal of time on his knees. You ask him the way to the Strand, and he tells you with perfect civility, and in the course of it you glance at the knees of his trousers. They are as you hoped. They are wrinkled, and stained, and worn through. You thank him, and go.

options.label: Walk Round the Block and Read the Bank Behind.
options.detail: A dull street, a bright one, and the corner of a bank. An assistant who spends his time in the cellar is digging towards something, and there is only one thing in the block worth reaching.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: The City and Suburban Bank, Coburg Branch. A cellar wall that backs onto the pawnbroker's cellar. The distance is four yards, and a man could dig it between ten and two in a fortnight.

options.outcome: You walk round the block twice, with your hands behind you, and your hat over your eyes. On the second turn you have the whole of it. The little shop is at the back of the bank. The assistant is digging. The League has been sitting at the other end of the town, for four pounds a week, in order that the shop should be empty every day from ten to two.

options.label: Send Watson to Ask at the Tobacconist's.
options.detail: A tobacconist sees everything on a corner. A doctor with a pipe may ask him for a light, and a question, and be given both.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: He says that the assistant goes out for a pipe every afternoon at two, Holmes, with a sooty face, and goes back in again. He volunteered it.

options.outcome: Watson is gone twenty minutes, and returns with a good cigar, a great deal of gossip, and a look of enormous, innocent satisfaction. He has, without in the least intending it, been told about the whole of the street. You tell him that he is an admirable detective, and he says, rather pink, that he does not think that he had better be told so by you in public.

echoes.text: The card from the office door is in your pocket-book. It is dated the ninth of October, and it was not written by anybody who expected to be read.

L3.title: A Concert and a Conference
L3.description:
Saturday 11 October 1890, the evening. Sarasate is playing at St James's Hall, and you have spent the afternoon in it, with your fingers moving a little in the air to the music, and your face as vacant as a child's. It is not a thing that Watson can ever quite believe.

At seven you are back at Baker Street, with a cold supper laid, and two gentlemen in the sitting-room: Mr Peter Jones of Scotland Yard, who is official and a little stiff, and Mr Merryweather, a director of the City and Suburban Bank, who is tall, sad and solemn, and does not at all like being out after dark. In the cellar of his bank, you have told them both, are thirty thousand napoleons in boxes.

options.label: Ask Mr Merryweather for the Vault Key and Be Dark About It.
options.detail: He will give it, because he is afraid to refuse. A key is a simple thing to forge, and a simple thing to be seen holding.

quote.speaker: Mr Merryweather
quote.text: I do not at all like the idea of a stranger in the vaults at night, Mr Holmes, with the French gold. But I have been a director for twenty years, and I have never been told anything by a man who looked so extremely sure of it.

options.outcome: He hands it over like a man giving up a relative. It is a long, heavy, ugly key, on a ring, and you slip it into your pocket and tell him that he will have it back by morning. He goes pale. Mr Jones says, in a low and carefully official voice, that he hopes that this is not a practical joke. You tell him that it is, in a sense, the last thing in the world that you would call it.

options.label: Press Mr Jones to Bring Four Men and Handcuffs.
options.detail: It is an old rule that a man who is walking into a trap should be given the benefit of company. The company had better be armed.

quote.speaker: Mr Peter Jones
quote.text: He is a clever fellow, is John Clay, Mr Holmes. His grandfather was a royal duke and he has been to Eton and Oxford. I have been on his track for years and have never set eyes on him yet. I shall bring four men, and a revolver, and I should be extremely obliged if you would lend me a little courage.

options.outcome: He says it with much dignity, and some resentment, and goes away at once to the nearest station to find the men. You are rather pleased. The Yard is slow and conventional, but it has a bulldog's courage and a bulldog's tenacity when it is once at close quarters, and you have, on the whole, a high opinion of Mr Jones.

options.label: Say That You Will Go Alone, and Ask Them to Wait at the Door.
options.detail: A crowd in a vault is a crowd that makes a noise. You have been alone in worse places, and rather like it.

quote.speaker: Mr Merryweather
quote.text: Alone, Mr Holmes? In my own bank, in the dark, with a thirty thousand pounds beneath the floor? I should prefer, if I may say so, to have the Yard in the room.

options.outcome: He is upset, and Mr Jones is affronted, and for a quarter of an hour the conversation is rather painful. You are obliged to say several times that it is not a lack of confidence in either of them. By the end of it you have a compromise: they are to be at the door of the bank, and you are to be in the cellar, and nobody is to be happy about it.

echoes.text: You can still see the trousers. There is a patch at the knee that nothing in the world but a spade can produce.
A map of four yards of London is drawn on the back of the concert-programme. You have done nothing better all week, and you did it during the Mendelssohn.
Watson is on the sofa, with a good cigar and an air of conscious usefulness, and does not in the least know why he is so pleased.

L4.title: The Cellar
L4.description: Saturday night, a little after ten. The cellar of the City and Suburban Bank is a long, cold, stone place, stacked to the roof with boxes and crates, and smelling of damp and old wood. You are on your knees with a lantern and a lens, and have been for an hour; Mr Jones is crouching behind a packing-case with a pair of handcuffs, and Mr Merryweather is behind another, holding his breath. At ten past, a thin, pale line of light appears between two flagstones in the floor, and spreads, and a flagstone rises, silently, as if on hinges. A hand comes through the opening, a white hand, quite small. It feels about, for a moment. It finds the edge of the floor. Then a face follows it, with a splash of white acid upon the forehead. A head of bright red hair, and the man, with a sigh, rolls up into the cellar and sits there with his legs over the edge.

options.label: Pounce on the First Man and Hold Him by the Wrist.
options.detail: He has a revolver in his pocket, and a rope over his shoulder, and he is as quick as a cat. You have a hunting-crop. It is a matter of the first half-second.

quote.speaker: John Clay
quote.text: It is no use, John. You have no chance at all. I have a man at the front, and a man at the back, and another at the door, and a large number of friends in this cellar who are all, I am happy to say, extremely patient.

success.outcome: The crop comes down on his wrist, and the pistol clatters on the stone, and Jones is across the floor like a terrier with the handcuffs before the other man's head is out of the hole. There is a cry, a scramble, a splash of loose earth, and a rush of feet along the tunnel. 'You will not gain much by that,' says Clay, with a good-humoured smile, 'for there are three of our friends at the door of the shop.' It is the neatest little arrest that you have ever seen.

failure.outcome: You are a half-second late. The hunting-crop goes through the air and meets the edge of the flagstone. The man is down the hole as if he had been dropped, with a lamp, and a spade, and a noise like a cat on a roof. By the time Jones has found the end of the tunnel in the shop, there is nothing in it but a smell of paraffin and a trail of boot-prints. The bank is a great deal poorer, and the gold, which had been in the boxes for a week, is in a cart.

options.label: Hold the Light Back and Let Mr Jones Take Them on the Stair.
options.detail: You have a man at the door of the shop, and four more behind the cellar-stair. You have only to keep the lantern shut.

quote.speaker: Mr Peter Jones
quote.text: I'll have him, Mr Holmes. I'll have the pair of them. I have been waiting for years for the chance of putting my hand upon the collar of John Clay, and I do not intend to ask you to do it for me.

options.outcome: He goes up the stair like a young man, with the four constables behind him, and takes the second one on the way out of the hole, with a shout, and a flurry, and a great quantity of dust. Clay himself he takes in the shop, in the dark, at the foot of the little ladder. It is entirely Mr Jones's affair, and he deserves the whole of the credit for it, and receives, from you, with an air of perfect sincerity, the whole of the congratulations.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs four men from the Yard

options.label: Take Clay Quietly and Let the Bank Say Nothing.
options.detail: A scandal would ruin the City and Suburban, and a quiet arrest would save it. It is not a thing that the papers need know.

quote.speaker: Mr Merryweather
quote.text: I should be everlastingly grateful, Mr Holmes, if the matter could be kept out of the Times. I have been a director for twenty years, and I do not at all like to think what my fellow directors would say.

options.outcome: It is done in the dark, in twenty minutes, without a shot. The two men are taken out by the back door of the shop in a four-wheeler, with a handkerchief round the mouth of one of them. The bank opens on Monday as usual. A paragraph, at the foot of the fifth column of the Standard, says that a quantity of coin was moved on Saturday night, for security.

options.label: Go Home to Bed and Leave the Bank to Mind Its Own Gold.
options.detail: It was a clever plan, and a good one. It will, you think, be a pity to spoil it.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Holmes, I really do not understand you. Do you mean to say that we are going home?

options.outcome: You rise from the packing-case, brush the dust from your knees, and say that it is a splendid night for a walk. You go home. In the morning, at ten, there is a long, white, terrible face at the door of Baker Street, and it belongs to Mr Merryweather.

options.label: Give Mr Wilson the Cellar Key and Let Him Wait at the Top of the Stair.
options.detail: He has told you all of it, and you have seen the knees of his assistant's trousers. A pawnbroker who has been robbed of his own cellar has, you think, much right to be the man standing over the hole.

quote.speaker: Jabez Wilson
quote.text: Me, Mr Holmes? In my own cellar? With my own umbrella? I do not at all know what I am to say. But I should be proud to be asked.

options.outcome: He is a stout, flushed, brave little man, and he takes up his post at the top of his own cellar steps with the family umbrella across his knees and an expression of immense and trembling dignity. At ten past ten a flagstone rises, and a head of red hair comes up through the floor, and Mr Jabez Wilson, who has never struck anyone in his life, brings down the umbrella, with both hands, upon the exact middle of it.
options.requiresHint: Needs Mr Wilson's whole story and the assistant's trousers seen

echoes.text: You are alone in the cellar, as you said you would be. You did not say it for the right reasons, and it is rather late to change your mind.
The whole of Jabez Wilson's story is in your head, in order, like a score. You have been listening to it for six hours.

SX1.title: Reading the River
SX1.description: Sunday 3 May, a flat grey morning. The Limehouse reach on a Sunday is shut and rather lovely, a long brown water with tarred sides moored along it, and not a crane moving. Wiggins has found a boat, and a man to row it, and has told the man that you are looking for a lost dog. You have two days, and a warehouse that you have so far seen only from the inside of a bad night. It is time to read the place the way that you read a hat. The river has been used for a good many years by a good many people, and it forgets nothing that is written on it.

options.label: Read the Tide Tables Against the Lighterman's Book.
options.detail: A barge comes up on the top of the tide or not at all. If the Professor has a ship, there is a day on which she will be there, and the book will say it.

quote.speaker: A lighterman
quote.text: The Teal comes up on the top of the tide on Tuesday, a quarter past eight, and she never takes a load. Not once in a year. Rides high as a cork, she does, and goes out as light as she came in.

options.outcome: He lends you the book, in a pub, with a pot of tea, and you go down the column with your finger. It takes half an hour. By the end of it you know the hour, to the quarter, at which the thing that is going to happen on Tuesday will happen. You know that there is a stair at the water's edge that will be dry at that hour and under water an hour afterwards.

options.label: Watch the Wharf From a Hired Barge.
options.detail: A man in a boat with a pipe is the least interesting thing on the river. You may lie off the water-stairs all morning.

quote.speaker: A bargee
quote.text: That's the third time that cart has been in and out since seven, guv'nor, and it's a Sunday. There's nothing to deliver on a Sunday.

options.outcome: You lie off the stairs with a line over the side and watch the gate in the way that a cat watches a hole. In three hours you see a cart, a small boy with a loaf, and a tall, stooping gentleman who does not come out again. It is not the Professor. It is someone who knows the Professor, and who walks in the way that a man walks who is sure of his welcome.

options.label: Ask the River Police Who Pays for the Moorings.
options.detail: A wharf is rented, and a lease is a name. The Thames Police keep a book, and the sergeant of the Wapping station owes Lestrade a favour.

quote.speaker: The sergeant at Wapping
quote.text: The lease is in the name of a Mr Alexander Bell, of nowhere, paid quarterly, in notes. I should be glad if somebody would tell me why a man pays a thousand a year for a warehouse that has never in four years had a cask of anything in it but oil.

options.outcome: He is delighted to be asked, and has been waiting for the better part of a year for somebody to ask. You leave with a copy of the lease, a plan of the foreshore and a promise that the Thames Police will be looking the other way on Tuesday at eight. It is not much.

SX2.title: The Chalk and the Lamp-Oil
SX2.description: Monday 4 May, noon. Wiggins and three of the boys are lying on the roof of a sugar-warehouse across the water-lane with their chins on their fists, and Alf has been sent to buy a pennyworth of toffee at a shop that has a view of the gate. The warehouse is a plain, high, flat-faced building with a hoist at the top and a double door at the bottom, and it has, in an ordinary light, nothing to say for itself at all. In the light of a Monday noon, with a lens, it has three things. There is chalk on the bollards. There are casks at the gate. And there is a carter who comes every day, at the same hour, with the same loaf.

options.label: Read the Chalk Marks on the Bollards.
options.detail: Three crosses and a bar, on every post from the stairs to the gate. It is not a child's game. It is the way that a thing is laid out in the dark.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: I told you, Mr Holmes. I'd not say it was a child that did it. A child would've drawn a face.

options.outcome: You go down the row with a lens and a pencil. They are not a child's. They are a route: the stairs, the gate, the yard, the door, a flight of steps that goes down and not up, and an arrow at the end of it. Someone who is not the Professor has laid out the way to a place in the building that he does not wish to be found in. It is the sort of thing that is useful only to the man who is expecting to be followed.

options.label: Count the Lamp-Oil Casks Through the Slats of the Gate.
options.detail: A warehouse that has never in four years held anything but oil has, on the Monday of the raid, more oil than it ever held. A fire is being prepared.

quote.speaker: Alf
quote.text: Forty-one, Mr Holmes, and I counted twice. And the ones at the back haven't got any of them tops on. I think they've been took off. They stink something dreadful.

options.outcome: You do not need to count them. You smell them from the far side of the lane, a sweet, rank, greasy smell that goes into the back of the throat. There is much more of it than a respectable warehouse would keep, and the casks have been moved, since Saturday, from the back of the building to the front. Somebody is not intending to leave the place as he found it. You write down forty-one, and underline it, and decide that you will need to know where the hoist-chain is.

options.label: Follow the Carter Who Brings the Bread.
options.detail: A man who brings bread to an empty warehouse every day at noon is feeding somebody. He may be feeding the man you want.

quote.speaker: The carter
quote.text: Gov'nor? I just brings the bread. A gentleman pays me a shilling at the Prince of Wales in Cable Street, and he's never said what he wants it for.

success.outcome: He has a bad cough, a dray with a weak wheel, and no instinct whatever for being followed. You are with him to the Prince of Wales and a hundred yards past it, and when he comes out you have the name of the gentleman who pays him, and the hour at which the gentleman collects the bread. It is a name that you do not know and a habit that you can use.

failure.outcome: He is a good deal less stupid than he looks. At the second corner he stops his dray, gets down, and stands looking at the horse's off hind hoof with an attention that no horse's hoof has ever merited, until you have gone past. When you look back he has gone. The bread has not been delivered.

echoes.text: In your pocket-book is the hour of the tide, to the quarter, and the name of a barge that never takes a load.
A copy of the lease is folded in your coat. It is in the name of a Mr Alexander Bell, who does not exist.

CX1.title: The Hotel Register
CX1.description: Monday 4 May, eight in the morning. It is a fine, hard morning, with the Alps standing up out of the valley like things that have been washed, and a smell of coffee and woodsmoke from the Englischer Hof. The Professor is somewhere on the line from Interlaken, and will be here before four. Before that, you have the hotel. You know, as you know the weather, that somebody will try today to separate you from Watson, and that the means will be a message, and that the message will be in a hand that is not the sender's. You have six hours, and a house full of people who are paid to be incurious.

options.label: Read the Hotel Register.
options.detail: A ledger of names, with a column for nationality and a column for the date. It will say who is here and who is not.

quote.speaker: The proprietor
quote.text: An English lady, Monsieur? Madame, I regret that there is no English lady in this house who is ill. There is a Mrs Fenwick of Bath, who is perfectly well, and a Miss Sutherland, who is out walking.

options.outcome: He is shocked, and then he is helpful. You go down the register with your finger. There is no English lady who is ill. There is none who has sent for a doctor. There is, at the foot of the page, a gentleman who arrived on Saturday with a small bag and a violin-case and who has taken the room immediately over the stair, and who is out.

options.label: Question the Stable-Boy About Who Has Hired the Guides.
options.detail: A guide is a man who knows where the path goes. It would be as well to know who has paid him to keep away.

quote.speaker: The stable-boy
quote.text: Hans has gone down to Interlaken, sir, with the other two, and he was told that he would not be wanted until the Wednesday. The gentleman paid him in gold. I have never seen so much gold in a week.

options.outcome: He tells it in the Swiss German of the valley, and more than a little it goes by, but the substance is plain. Every guide in Meiringen who could have told you the path has been paid to be somewhere else. It is an economical piece of work: not one threat, and not one lie. The Professor has simply, and with great politeness, bought the whole of a village.

options.label: Look at the Forms at the Telegraph Office.
options.detail: A forged message has to be written, and written on something. The little office at the foot of the street keeps its forms.

quote.speaker: The telegraph clerk
quote.text: The message for the English doctor? It was handed in at half past ten, Monsieur, at the counter, by a boy. It was written in pencil, on one of our forms, with a good English hand. It was not, I think, written by a lady.

options.outcome: You turn over the copies of the morning's messages, which he is extremely reluctant to let you see and perfectly willing to let you see for a franc. It is there: a request, in a clear and rather mannered English, for Dr Watson to come at once to the hotel at the foot of the Falls. The writing is the writing of a man who has been told what a woman's handwriting looks like. You put it in your pocket-book beside the ticket, and you underline the time.

echoes.text: Mrs Norton's warning is in your head like a small cold coin. A message, in the morning, for the Doctor. You have not told Watson. You intend to.
At the foot of the stair, with a book, a lady in grey is reading the same page that she was reading at dinner. She does not look up.

CX2.title: The Path in Daylight
CX2.description: Monday 4 May, ten in the morning. The path above the Reichenbach is a path of rock and wet roots, cut into the side of the gorge, going up and round through the spruce. It ends at a broad flat ledge on the lip of the upper fall, and the ledge ends in nothing at all. It is the loveliest and the least comfortable place that you have ever been. By dusk it will be the place where one of two men will not be. Now it is a place in a book. You have an hour, a walking-stick, and the knowledge that you will not be given another chance to look at it.

options.label: Walk the Path to the Fall and Read the Ground.
options.detail: A path is a record. Every man who has gone along it has left something, and the wet makes it last.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: Two sets of prints up, since the rain: a heavy boot, a light boot. None down. And at the ledge a place where the moss has been scraped by a heel, in the way that a man scrapes it who is preparing to be thrown.

options.outcome: You go up in the cold, with the roar of the water growing, and stand on the ledge with your toes at the edge. It is a hundred and sixty feet to the black water and a cloud of spray comes up over the lip in slow, soft puffs. Nothing could be quieter than the place where a man will die. On the way down you notice two things: the path is much wider than it looks, and in one place, at a bend, it is not very much wider than a man.

options.label: Find the Cleft in the Rock Below the Ledge.
options.detail: There is a place at the foot of the cliff-face where a small man might go over the edge of the path and not be seen from the ledge. It will want a rope, and plenty of care.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are going over the edge of a cliff, Holmes, with a rope, in a pair of boots that were bought for Bond Street. I should like to be told what you propose to find there.

options.outcome: It takes the whole hour, and more than a little language. But you find it: a narrow cleft in the rock, a few feet below the lip of the path, with a ledge that will take the weight of a man lying flat. A root as thick as your wrist to hold by. From the path above it is invisible. You lie in it for a full minute, with the spray on your face and the sky going round, and feel, for the first time in a week, calm.

options.label: Leave the Path Unread and Rest Before the Afternoon.
options.detail: You will need your head by four, and a man who has walked a cliff-path in the morning has not got one.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I am extremely glad to hear it, Holmes. I was beginning to think that you would not sleep again until you had gone over the edge yourself.

options.outcome: You go back to the hotel and lie on the bed with your boots on and your hands behind your head, and for two hours you do not think about anything at all. It is the nearest thing to a prayer that you have said for years. Watson looks in, once, and goes away again on tiptoe, with a face of such tender concern that you are obliged to pretend to be asleep.

echoes.text: Somewhere in the Englischer Hof there is a man with a violin-case, who has taken a room over the stair and is, at present, out.
There is not a guide in the valley who will tell you where the path is wide and where it is narrow. You are left to your own legs, and the spruces.

AC.title: The Lady in Grey
AC.description: Sunday 3 May, ten at night. A knock at the door of your room at the Englischer Hof, and it is not the knock of a servant. It is a short, rapid, businesslike rap, and when you open the door there is a lady in a grey travelling-dress, with a veil put back, who says that she is sorry to disturb you and not at all sorry to have found you. You last saw her at Briony Lodge, on the day she burned a packet in a pair of tongs. She is paler, and a little thinner, and she has the air of having walked a great way in order to say a thing that she has been a long time rehearsing. It is Mrs Norton, and she has not come for the view.

options.label: Hear Her Warning About a Message.
options.detail: She has been in the hotel two days, and has been listening. A woman at a table with a book hears everything.

quote.speaker: Mrs Norton
quote.text: There is a boy in the yard who has been paid a franc to run with a message at noon tomorrow. I have not seen the message. I have seen the man who wrote it. He was tall, and he walked as if he had been in India. He did not at any point look at me, which I thought was unusual in a man who had been staring at the door for an hour.

options.outcome: She says it in four sentences, as she would give evidence, and she does not ask for anything. You thank her, and she says that thanks are unnecessary, in a tone that suggests that they are, on the contrary, extremely necessary and that she is a good deal too proud to say so. You have, at the end of it, a time and a description and a face. You also have, distinctly, the feeling of having been given something that you cannot pay for.

options.label: Ask Her to Watch the Hotel in the Morning.
options.detail: A woman at a table with a book is the best watcher in Europe. She will see who comes to the desk and who goes to the stable.

quote.speaker: Mrs Norton
quote.text: You wish me to sit in the hall and read my book, and to remember who goes past. I think it is the only thing that I am really good at. Yes.

options.outcome: She agrees at once, and without the least show of reluctance, and goes away to her room with the lamp. You hear her door close, and, a little after, the faint, domestic sound of a woman winding a watch. You sleep, which you had not expected, and in the morning you find that the chair at the foot of the stair has been occupied since six, by a lady in grey, with a book, who does not look up.

options.label: Thank Her and Send Her Back to Brussels.
options.detail: The Professor is not a man who forgives an accomplice. She has done a great deal already, and it would be wrong to let her do more.

quote.speaker: Mrs Norton
quote.text: You are sending me away. I thought that you might. It is all right. You are being kind, and I am not at all accustomed to being protected, and I find that I do not like it. But I shall go.

options.outcome: She goes down the stairs in the grey dress with her bag in her hand, as if she were leaving a theatre. You watch her from the window all the way to the station. She does not look back. In the morning, at the desk, there is a note for you in a firm hand, in violet ink. It says, 'Quite so,' and nothing else, and you keep it, with the other one.

AY.title: A Witness From St John's Wood
AY.description: Thursday 11 June, a little after nine in the morning. A note was left at Baker Street in the night, on violet paper, in a hand that you know. It says that Mr Hector Dunmore of Brandt and Chambers has been seen with a certain gentleman in the neighbourhood of the Old Bailey, and that she has, in consequence, taken it upon herself to walk across London on a wet morning and stand in the corner of Lestrade's room until somebody gives her a chair. She is there when you arrive, in the grey dress, on the hard chair, with her gloves in her lap. Lestrade is looking at her with the fixed, wary civility of a man who has been told that a lady is a witness and has not yet been told what for.

options.label: Take Her Sealed Statement to Lestrade's Desk.
options.detail: She has written it down, in a firm hand, in the order in which it happened. It names the buyer and the bank. It is the first piece of evidence in the case that a jury might look at twice.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: I don't know what to make of her, Mr Holmes, and that's the truth. I'd be obliged if you'd tell the lady that I'm much obliged.

options.outcome: She signs it with a flourish, at the Inspector's blotter, and he reads it standing, with his lips moving. At the end he folds it into his inside pocket beside the warrants, and pats it, and looks at you with the beginnings of respect. It is, you reflect, an extraordinary thing, that two such different people should have found, in the course of five minutes, that they liked one another.

options.label: Tell Her to Stay Out of Court and Out of London.
options.detail: She has done enough. The Professor's people have a long memory, and a witness is a person who can be found.

quote.speaker: Mrs Norton
quote.text: You are trying to protect me. You may tell Mr Lestrade that I am sorry to have wasted his chair.

options.outcome: She rises, shakes hands with the Inspector, who has never in his life shaken the hand of a lady in a Scotland Yard office and is plainly not sure what to do with his thumb, and goes out. You see her to a cab. In the doorway she turns, and says that she has a feeling that you are going to be unhappy for a little time, and that she would very much like it if you did not do it alone. Then the cab goes, and the rain.

options.label: Ask Her to Dine With Mr Dunmore.
options.detail: It is a dangerous request and a good plan. She is the only person in London who can be in a room with him and be expected.

quote.speaker: Mrs Norton
quote.text: You wish me to dine with the man who tried to buy my letters, and to be charming, and to find out where he keeps the rest of the money. It is a long time since I was asked to do something that mattered.

success.outcome: She is at a table for two at the Café Royal at eight, in black, with a diamond at the throat, and she is much more charming than a man in his position has any right to expect. By the second course he has told her the name of his clerk and the number of his box. By the fourth he has let slip the day, and the hour, and the door. She comes out into Regent Street at eleven with a headache and a handful of facts, and gives you all of them in a cab.

failure.outcome: She is at the table for two, and she is as charming as the evening requires, and at the fifth course he leans across and says, pleasantly, that he knows who she is, and who has sent her, and that he is extremely sorry for her. He pays the bill and goes. She walks home alone through the rain. You find the note under your door in the morning. It says: 'I am not hurt. I should like it noted that I was not at all frightened.'

echoes.text: She is a good deal calmer than the room. She sits with her gloves in her lap, as one sits in a waiting-room at a dentist's, and looks at the Inspector's inkwell with polite interest.

Y9D.title: The Chase Along the Towpath
Y9D.description: Saturday 20 June, half past three in the morning. The net has not closed. At the last moment the tall, stooping figure on the towpath has seen the lantern on the bridge, and has turned and gone along the cut at a great pace, with his head thrust forward and his coat flying, and is already a hundred yards off. It is a black, narrow, wet night, with the towpath running between a high wall and the water, and every second that you stand here is a second in which he is further away. This is not the end. You can do one thing more. Whatever you have prepared in the last two months will be needed in the next ten minutes.

options.label: Send the Constables Ahead to the Lock.
options.detail: You have a man on the lock, because you set one there. He will be standing with a lantern in the middle of the path when the Professor arrives.
options.outcome: The Professor comes round the bend at a steady walk, with his hat in his hand and a face of perfect composure, and finds a constable standing in the lock-gate with a lantern. He stops. He looks at the constable, and then, slowly, over his shoulder, at the three men coming along the path behind him, and then he puts his hat on again, with some care, and says that he supposes there is no help for it.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs a watch set on the canal

options.label: Whistle for the Boys on the Roofs.
options.detail: A boy on a roof can see the whole length of the cut. If you have the hands, you have the eyes.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: He's gone along the wall, Mr Holmes! Alf's got him, he's on the shed roof! He's gone left! He's gone left!

options.outcome: The whistle goes up and down the length of the canal, from roof to roof, like a thing that is alive. In a minute there is a cry, and then another, and then a string of small, triumphant voices. The Professor, who has been going along the cut at a great pace with every sense alert, finds himself pursued from above by thirteen children and a dog. He is not a man who runs well. He is a very much better man at sitting.
options.requiresHint: Needs Hands in hand

options.label: Run Him Down Yourself.
options.detail: A hundred yards in the dark, on a wet towpath, after a man ten years older than you. It is the kind of thing that you do rather well.

quote.speaker: Professor Moriarty
quote.text: You are persistent, Mr Holmes. It is a fault in the young, and a virtue, I am told, in the dog.

success.outcome: You are on him at the bend, in a flat run, with the stick under your arm, and you take him by the collar of the coat before he knows that you are there. He does not struggle. He stops, still, and stands with his head swaying slowly from side to side, in the light of the lantern, and says, mildly, that he had not supposed that you would be so fast. Behind you the constables come up with a rush.

failure.outcome: You are twenty yards short when the dark puts a root across your path. You go down on your face on the wet stone, with the wind knocked out of you, and by the time that you are up there is nothing at the end of the towpath at all but a cab, with its lamps lit, driving fast and quite silently towards the City.

options.label: Let Him Go.
options.detail: You have not the means to stop him. There are better ways to be a policeman than to chase an old man along a canal.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: You are letting him go, Mr Holmes. I do not understand it. But I'll say nothing, if you say nothing, and we'll both go home to bed.

options.outcome: You stand with your hands in your pockets and watch him go, a tall, stooping figure that grows smaller and smaller along the cut, until it passes under the next bridge and is gone. Your career holds no more dignified retreat, and no more expensive one.

S8D.title: The Fire on the Stair
S8D.description: Tuesday night, the lamp-light flickering. The first of the oil casks goes up with a low, soft roar, and the whole of the dim, high place is suddenly, shockingly bright. The Professor has not been trying to defend the warehouse. He has been trying to burn it, and he has done it with the thing that he has been collecting for a week. There is a river of burning oil spreading along the floor, a hoist-chain swinging in the heat, and fifteen boys, a small boy among them, in a building with only two doors. You have, perhaps, three minutes, and a great deal to lose.
